chapters.summary: Chair Selvena Brooks-Powers welcomes attendees and identifies the committee, herself as chair, and the bills being heard: Intro 809, Intro 453, and Intro 133. She notes members joining and frames the hearing around mental health care in city jails.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers opens hearing and introduces mental health oversight bills

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And good morning once again.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I am still Councilmember Silvina Brooks-Powers, and I am the Chair of the Committee on Criminal Justice.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I want to welcome everyone to today's hearing on mental health care in New York City jails.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The committee will also be hearing introduction number 809, sponsored by myself, in relation to requiring the Department of Correction to create and implement policies to address medical needs during and after lock-ins.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Introduction 453, sponsored by Councilmember Stevens, in relation to the provision of mental health services for children visiting incarcerated individuals.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And introduction number 133, sponsored by Councilmember Kavan, in relation to extending the minimum duration of and updating other requirements pertaining to the task force

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: created to address policies related to the treatment and housing of transgender, gender nonconforming, nonbinary, and intersex individuals in the custody of the Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I am joined by Council Members Murano, Narcisse,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Brewer, and come on.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says about 60% of people in city jails have a documented mental health need, with one in five having serious mental illness. She outlines the continuum of care to be examined, including mental observation, PACE, and outposted therapeutic housing units.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers frames jail mental health crisis and care continuum

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The issue before us today reflects one of the most significant challenges facing our city's jail system.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Ensuring that people in custody with mental health needs receive appropriate care while navigating a system that was never designed to serve as a substitute for a comprehensive behavioral or mental health system.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Today, approximately 60% of people in city jails have a documented mental health need, and approximately one in five people in custody has been identified as having a serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: For many New Yorkers in custody, incarceration has become the point at which they first receive consistent access to mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Specialized units and treatment models exist, but the prevalence of serious mental illness in our jails raises important questions about whether individuals are receiving care at the appropriate level.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: whether treatment is accessible when needed, and whether the current system is equipped to support people with complex behavioral health needs.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: People experiencing serious mental illness may require consistent medication, management, therapeutic services, and specialized housing to prevent further deterioration.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When access to care is disrupted, whether because of missed appointments, staffing challenges, housing limitations, or operational issues, those disruptions can have serious implications for individuals'health and safety.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Today's hearing will examine the continuum of mental health care available within city jails, including mental

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: observation units, programs to accelerate clinical effectiveness or PACE units, and the city's new outposted therapeutic housing units.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We will examine how these programs function, how individuals are identified for placement, how quickly they can access appropriate levels of care, and whether existing capacity meets the needs of the current jail population.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says the committee will examine how lock-ins affect medical and mental health appointments. She stresses that continuity of care is critical for people with serious mental illness who rely on consistent treatment.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers highlights lock-ins disrupting treatment access

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The committee will also examine concerns regarding access to treatment during jail operations, including the impact of lock-ins on medical and mental health appointments.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When individuals are unable to access scheduled care, particularly

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: those with serious mental illness who rely on consistent treatment.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: It is critical that there are clear procedures to ensure a continuity of care.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers argues that closing Rikers and transitioning to borough-based jails requires reducing the jail population and meeting mental health needs. She says treatment, discharge planning, and diversion are necessities for the closure plan.
chapters.title: Chair links mental health care to Rikers closure and diversion

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As the city works towards closing Rikers Island and transitioning to a borough-based jail system, these questions take on added urgency.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: This transition can only happen successfully if our jail population is reduced and if a substantial share of the population is not having their mental health needs met, then we are not moving towards our goal.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Meeting these needs through treatment inside our jails today, through discharge planning, and through diversion to keep people out of custody in the first place is not separate from the closure plan.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: It is a necessity for it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: For that reason, today's hearing aims to better this council's understanding on how mental health care is provided to the individuals currently housed in our jails

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and what additional investments or reforms are needed to ensure that incarceration does not become the default response to unmet behavioral health needs.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers thanks committee staff by name and previews a productive discussion on strengthening jail mental health care. She then pauses to allow Council Member Cabán to give remarks on her bill.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers thanks staff and yields to Council Member Cabán

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I would like to thank my staff and committee staff for their hard work.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Jahari Frazier, counsel to the committee.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Chad Benjamin, policy analyst.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Casey Lasky, financial analyst.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Owen Brady, my policy and budget director.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And Renee Taylor, my chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I look forward to a productive discussion about how we can strengthen mental health care within our jail system, improve access to treatment, and ensure that New Yorkers in custody receive the support and services they need.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: With that, I am going to pause to allow Councilmember Kaban to give remarks pertaining to her bill.

chapters.summary: Council Member Tiffany Cabán says Rikers is especially dangerous for trans, non-binary, gender nonconforming, and intersex people. She describes denial of gender-aligned housing, discrimination, and violence she saw as a public defender.
chapters.title: Cabán warns of dangers for trans and gender nonconforming people on Rikers

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Entering Rikers Island is a potential death sentence for any New Yorker, but that is doubly true for trans, non-binary, and gender non-conforming people who are incarcerated there.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And on top of the other dangers and indignities of incarceration at Rikers, trans, gender non-conforming, non-binary, and intersex individuals are routinely denied access to housing that matches their gender identity.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: They're forced to live in an environment where they face discrimination and the risk of violence.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I saw that firsthand in my time as a public defender.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You know, it's unconscionable that in this city we are treating queer folks like this.

chapters.summary: Cabán credits the TGNC-NBI task force for exposing conditions in DOC custody and calls for passing Intro 133 to extend its mandate. She also says Intro 134 would give incarcerated New Yorkers recourse to safe gender-aligned housing.
chapters.title: Cabán promotes Intro 133 task force extension and Intro 134 housing protections

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The Task Force on Issues Faced by TGNC-NBI People in Custody has already done crucial oversight to bring this to the attention of council members, members of the administration, community-based organizations, and the public at large.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Their 2022 report did remarkable work bringing the experiences of trans and non-binary New Yorkers in DOC custody to light.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Their work is so vital because we cannot pass legislation without understanding the nature and scale of the issue at hand.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: They need not just a mandate, but our full support.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that is why it is essential that we pass my bill, Intro 133, to extend this task force and ensure that the DOC and Correctional Health Services substantively participate in its work.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I want to say that alongside Intro 133, I've also put forward Intro 134, which would give New Yorkers incarcerated at Rikers recourse to be housed in units where they will be safe from gender-based and sex-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so I hope that we can consider that bill to act on the recommendations of the task force.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you to Chair Brooks Powers and to my colleagues for supporting the bill, the folks that have signed on, and I'm really glad that it's being heard today.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Dr. Joseph Otonichar of Correctional Health Services introduces himself and colleague Jeanette Merrill. He says about 61% of patients receive mental health services and 22% have serious mental illness, with higher prevalence among women.
chapters.title: Dr. Otonichar introduces CHS and mental health prevalence in jails

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Brooks Powers and members of the committee on criminal justice.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: My name is Dr.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Joseph Otonakar.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I serve as the Chief of Mental Health for New York City Health and Hospitals Correctional Health Services.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I'm joined by my CHS colleague, Jeanette Merrill, Senior Assistant Vice President of Communications and External Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We appreciate the opportunity to testify today on mental health care in the New York City jails, an issue of paramount importance.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Since 2016, CHS has been the direct provider of physical and mental health services to people in the custody of the New York City Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Approximately 61% of these individuals, our patients, have received mental health services during their incarceration, and about 22% of the total patient population has been diagnosed with a serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: The prevalence of mental illness is greater among women, with 85% of our female patients enrolled in the mental health service and 49% of our female patients diagnosed with a serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: The challenges and stressors of jail incarceration, which include restrictions on autonomy and control, can prove clinically destabilizing for many of our patients.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: The circumstances of pretrial detention can be chaotic and unpredictable and can exacerbate or even induce symptoms of psychological distress.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Uncertainty about the outcomes of legal cases can create additional tension and anxiety.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And this is all occurring at a time when our patients'access to community supports and outlets for coping are reduced.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Nonetheless, many of New York City's most clinically complex individuals receive mental health care on Rikers Island that they may not have had access to in the community.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: CHS recognizes the opportunity we have to care for this vulnerable population and works to ensure that all of our patients have access to high quality mental health services during what can be the most challenging time of their lives.

chapters.summary: Otonichar describes comprehensive medical intake and mental health referrals. He says clinicians review history, interview patients, seek collateral information, and use records including PSYCKES to determine diagnosis, treatment, and level of care.
chapters.title: Otonichar explains intake and mental health assessment process

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: In my testimony, I will provide an overview of CHS's mental health services, starting with the initial mental health assessment and concluding with our reentry services.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I will describe the spectrum of mental health care in the jails, including the mental health therapeutic housing units.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: CHS medical and nursing professionals conduct a comprehensive medical evaluation of all individuals when they are admitted to the New York City jail system.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: During these intake evaluations, nurses and doctors obtain vital signs, draw labs, and offer testing for communicable diseases.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: They also ask patients a comprehensive set of questions about their medical and mental health history and current physical and mental health status.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Based on the information obtained during the intake assessment, patients may be referred for follow-up care and or additional evaluations, including to the mental health service.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Patients may be referred to the mental health service for evaluation either as a result of the CHS intake screening or at any time during their incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: During every initial mental health assessment, a licensed CHS mental health provider reviews the patient's full mental health history, interviews the patient, and reviews an extensive social history with the patient, including

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: past personal relationships, educational attainment, adverse past experiences, and socioeconomic stressors.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Clinicians may obtain collateral information from community-based providers to inform their assessment and to ensure that the patient's history is complete and accurate.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: When available, the clinical mental health staff review past medical records as well as the patient's psychiatric services and clinical knowledge enhancement system or

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: psyches report, which includes historical information about inpatient psychiatric care at a New York State Office of Mental Health facility and Medicaid-funded community-based mental health treatment.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: The information the mental health provider obtains during this assessment helps to inform their diagnostic assessment, individualized treatment plan, case management, and reentry planning.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: The information also enables clinicians to assess clinical risk factors and to determine the patient's most appropriate mental health level of care.

chapters.summary: Otonichar explains that most patients with mental health needs are housed in general population and seen in clinics. He details specialized units including 17 mental observation units, the STEP program, 10 PACE units, and a 20-bed PACE unit at Bellevue.
chapters.title: Otonichar describes GP, MO, STEP, PACE, and Bellevue care levels

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Most patients who have mental health needs in the jail system are appropriately housed in the general population, or GP, and meet with mental health clinicians in the clinic for their appointments similar to an outpatient model of care in the community.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: The jail-based mental health therapeutic housing units, conversely, are designed for patients who have more robust mental health needs and require increased clinical observation and care coordination.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: These units offer a continuum of care leading up to units that are akin to residential treatment facilities in the community, with CHS mental health staff primarily working on the units to provide enhanced treatment interventions.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: For patients who benefit from a level of care higher than outpatient general population, CHS established mental observation or MO units, of which there are currently 17.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Patients on MO units are rounded on regularly by mental health

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: and received enhanced clinical monitoring and support.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Earlier this year, CHS also implemented the Supportive Transitional Engagement Program, or STEP, within the Mental Health Therapeutic Housing Continuum.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: STEP serves as an intermediary level of care between MO and GP.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: The most intensive level of mental health care CHS provides on Rikers Island is the Program to Accelerate Clinical Effectiveness, or PACE.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: These units house clinically vulnerable patients who have the most complex mental health needs, including persons with serious mental illness and or developmental disabilities, for whom a lower level of care is not optimal.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: There are currently 10 PACE units in operation, including a 20-bed PACE unit within the outposted therapeutic housing unit at Bellevue Hospital that houses patients who have comorbid psychiatric and medical complexities.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Within each of our PACE units, a multidisciplinary team, which includes mental health clinicians, creative arts therapists, treatment aides, and social work and nursing staff, works with each patient to provide coordinated care.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: CHS mental health clinicians continuously assess the patient's therapeutic needs throughout the individual's time in jail.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: As those needs change, CHS works with DOC to more appropriately house that individual.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: If a patient requires a higher level of care than can be offered in the jail setting, CHS initiates transfer to an

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: acute psychiatric hospital for evaluation and possible admission.

chapters.summary: Otonichar describes CHS reentry services, including Medicaid enrollment, community provider connections, medication access, and resources like CRAN, Portline, and PORT practices. He says patients with serious mental illness are offered supportive housing applications and other supports.
chapters.title: Otonichar details CHS reentry and discharge planning services

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Like all of CHS's patient care services, the Mental Health Service closely collaborates with CHS's Reentry and Transition Service to help connect patients to clinical resources in the community and to help ensure continuity of care upon discharge from jail.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: CHS makes core reentry services available to all patients and provides individualized discharge plans to patients with particular clinical needs, including all consenting patients receiving mental health treatment.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Reentry staff work to ensure that at a minimum, patients have Medicaid, a community provider, access to medication, and awareness of a variety of safety net resources.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: These resources include but are not limited to CHS Community Reentry Assistance Network, or CRAN, which helps former patients access community-based health and social services.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: CHS's peer staff general helpline called Portline, which helps people navigate community-based services, and the Point of Reentry and Transition, or PORT, practices located at New York City Health and Hospitals Bellevue

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: and Kings County Hospitals, which provide primary care, mental health care, and wraparound services to formerly incarcerated individuals.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We also invite all patients to drop into CHS's reentry services center on the visitor side of Rikers Island after their release.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Patients with serious mental illness are offered a

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: services including 2010 E supportive housing applications transitional case management services and free smartphones with a year-long service plan

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: the reentry team also works closely with partners in New York City government to help support our patients when they return to the community

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: For example, CHS refers patients as appropriate to the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene's Single Point of Access, or SPOA, program,

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: which connects people to intensive mobile treatment, assertive community treatment, and other such community-based programs.

chapters.summary: Otonichar says CHS provides community-standard care in a difficult environment for a marginalized population. He commits to working with the council and others to improve the system and says he is happy to take questions.
chapters.title: Otonichar concludes CHS testimony and offers questions

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: In conclusion, so many of our patients enter our care with tremendous sociomedical and mental health needs, and their involvement in the criminal legal system up to and including jail detention often exacerbates those challenges.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: CHS is proud to provide the community standard of care in a difficult environment to one of the city's most marginalized and vulnerable populations.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We remain committed to working with this city council and other stakeholders to improve the system and to support our patients before and after incarceration because we recognize that the challenges they face extend beyond the carceral walls.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Happy to take any questions.

chapters.summary: James Boyd introduces himself as Deputy Commissioner of Quality Assurance and Compliance at DOC and notes Assistant Chief Joseph Caputo. He says DOC ensures access to care through escorts, transportation, housing coordination, staff training, and modernization like the clinic production dashboard.
chapters.title: Deputy Commissioner Boyd introduces DOC role in jail mental health access

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Brooks Powers and members of the Committee on Criminal Justice.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: My name is James Boy, and I'm the Deputy Commissioner of Quality Assurance and Compliance at the New York City Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I'm joining you in a new role overseeing a new portfolio of work, which includes health affairs.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Joining me today is my colleague, Assistant Chief Joseph Caputo.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: My colleagues and I thank you for the opportunity to discuss this important topic and share how the department facilitates access to mental health care within our jails.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: New York City jails exist within a continuum of support, intervention, and care that is shared between many stakeholders and partners.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Our responsibility to people in our care includes making sure they receive access to medical and mental health treatment.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: They need to support their well-being while in our care.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: That responsibility is central to building a safer and more humane jail system.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Which is why Mayor Mumdani's administration has been laser focused on strengthening access to mental health services for people in our city's jails.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Our partners at Correctional Health Services bring the clinical expertise and our dedicated staff makes access possible by escorting people to the clinic, transporting them to outside appointments, and supporting the safe delivery of care within clinical spaces.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: In addition, DOC coordinates with CHS to ensure the smooth operation of

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: safe and inclusive housing options to meet a wide spectrum of mental health needs and all uniformed staff receive training to help them better understand and engage with individuals who have mental health needs while keeping them safe.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: That important work requires daily coordination from all levels of both agencies.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Behind each appointment is a person whose health matters, and our collective work must be measured by whether that person received the care they need.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: The department will continue prioritizing various modernization projects, including the clinic production dashboard, to improve processes and make this work more efficient.

chapters.summary: Boyd says DOC values the TGNC-NBI task force and wants collaboration to continue. He supports children having mental health access but says DOC is not the best agency to provide or refer those services, and he describes escorting patients during emergency lock-ins when safe.
chapters.title: Boyd comments on Intros 133, 453, and 809

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: The legislation before the committee speaks to that same responsibility.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Intro 133 concerns people whose safety and dignity require our sustained attention.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We value the task force contributions and the experience that advocates and community partners bring to improving the treatment and housing of transgender, gender nonconforming, nonbinary, and intersex people in our care.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: The feedback and collaboration that has been born out of these meetings has resulted in meaningful changes to practices within our jails.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We want that collaboration to remain strong and look forward to further conversations.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Intro 453 recognized that incarceration also affects children and families.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: A child visiting a parent deserves to feel welcome, supported, and safe.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Department has worked diligently over the past few years to build on our family-centered visiting initiatives and has worked with partners whose expertise has helped children and families receive targeted support

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: and attention so that visitation is meaningful and relationships remain intact.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: While we agree that children should have access to mental health services should they need it,

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We do not believe that the department is the best agency to offer those services or make referrals to such services.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Intro 809 addresses access to care during emergency lock-ins.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Protecting people from immediate harm and meeting their health care needs are both essential responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: In recognition of this, the department continues to escort individuals to medical appointments during emergency lock-ins

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: when it is safe to do so and coordinates closely with CHS to address any clinic encounters that may have been missed as a result of a lock-in, often as soon as the same day.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We look forward.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: To working with CHS and the council to address any remaining gaps to ensure that people continue to have access to the services that they need.

chapters.summary: Boyd says the administration is committed to community safety and access to vital services in custody. He says DOC is working with the Remediation Manager and Federal Monitor and welcomes questions.
chapters.title: Boyd commits to monitor coordination and closes DOC testimony

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: This administration is committed to an approach that puts community safety at the center of all the work we do.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: That means we share a responsibility to ensure people in our city's jail have access to vital services that support their dignity, safety, and health, and to work in partnership with all stakeholders along the continuum from upstream divergence

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: efforts to post-release community-based care to work towards better outcomes.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: As we often say, there is more work ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We are eager to build on improvements that are already underway, and we are working closely in coordination with the Remediation Manager and Federal Monitor and their respective teams to ensure they are part of the process as we move forward.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Thank you again for inviting us to discuss these important matters.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We welcome any questions you may have at this time.

chapters.summary: Chair Brooks-Powers notes Council Member Althea Stevens has joined to speak on her legislation. Stevens says children visiting incarcerated parents experience trauma and deserve mental health referrals, citing her work with young people and a visit to Horizon.
chapters.title: Chair recognizes Council Member Stevens on Intro 453 for children of incarcerated parents

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'd like to add that we've been joined by Councilmember Stevens, who will give some remarks regarding her legislation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Good morning and thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm honored to be here today for Intro 453 legislation that speaks directly to our responsibility to protect and support children and families.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Children visiting incarcerated parents or family members can experience fear, confusion, sadness, and anxiety, and trauma that often goes unaddressed.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: As a city, we have the responsibility to make sure that these young people have access to the supports they need and to process those experiences in a healthy way.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This legislation actually came about as most people know that I worked with young people for over 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And for a multiple number of years, young people who had family members, particularly parents who were experiencing incarceration, would come to my programs with severe trauma.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: One of my young people that I worked with actually came to me and helped me develop this even before I was in council to say, I wish I would have had someone to talk to.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I wish someone would have been there to process what I experienced and tell me that I was going to be okay because they were like their parent was never coming home.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This young person's father was facing life in prison and did not know how to process that at such a young age.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so this legislation is very near and dear to me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So when talking about incarceration, we can not only focus on the person who's incarcerated, we have to think about the children and the family who are also impacted.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is why Intro 453 is so important.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This legislation would ensure that

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: that children visiting incarcerated individuals could receive referrals to mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: As the chair of the Committee on Children and Youth, I believe that our work must always center the well-being of our young people.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We have to meet young people where they are and provide them with the support before trauma becomes a deeper crisis.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Me and my colleagues visited yesterday Horizon, and we saw hundreds of children who were in secure detention.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And that was because a lot of them did not know how to process trauma.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So this is a way and a step that I believe that could help with some of that prevention.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If we're serious about breaking the cycles of harm of incarceration, then we must invest in healing, family stability, and prevention.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Every child deserves the opportunity to process their difficult experience with care, compassion, professional support, especially at a time where young people continue to ask for greater access to mental health.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When young people tell us what they need, we have the responsibility to listen to them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And more importantly, we must deliver what they're asking for.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Intro 453 is about recognizing that incarceration impacts entire families and supporting children is an essential part of building healthier and safer communities.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I want to thank my colleagues for supporting this and this important legislation, and I urge everyone to continue to support this.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says the hearing was noticed 21 days earlier and that she asked for testimony at least 24 hours in advance. She tells Boyd the administration's failure to submit timely testimony is disrespectful and hinders preparation. Boyd acknowledges the feedback and says he will take it back.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers presses administration on late testimony and hearing notice

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you for convening yesterday's tour of Horizon.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: It was definitely insightful.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay, let's get into it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: First things first.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Commissioner, can you let me know when this hearing was noticed?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do you recall when this hearing was noticed?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Are you asking when do we receive notification?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I mean, I receive it internally, so I got it from our, you know, our intergovernmental team, so I don't recall the actual date.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do you guys normally get it before it's put publicly?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: That I'm not totally aware of.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I think we normally see a public notification first, but I'm not.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I think it's coordinated in terms of the date to make sure that the administration is available.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I ask that because we noticed this hearing on September 2nd, 21 days ago.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I also requested that when coming to this hearing, and I can't speak for any other committee, that we have testimony at least 24 hours in advance.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I ask this so that we can have a meaningful conversation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I'm going to say publicly on the record what I have said privately to the administration.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The past administration was able to submit testimony in advance.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The MTA, which is a state agency, was able to submit testimony in advance.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I imagine this administration has the capacity to be able to submit testimony 24 hours in advance so that I can properly be prepared to chair this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I do feel it's very disrespectful that I continue to have that request disregarded.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I feel like it's showing that the administration does not have good faith to work together to have a

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: truly productive conversation during these hearings because it allows us an opportunity to prepare better and not have redundant questions that you may be addressing in your testimony anyway and have to do that in real time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I really want to maximize the use of my colleagues'time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Your time is mine.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I'm going to say it on the record again.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: My request is that going forward, any agency that comes before the Committee on Criminal Justice has testimony to us within 24 hours of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And I just want to acknowledge that, and I'm happy to take that feedback.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Obviously, you've had a conversation.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I've spoken to them, too, yep.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: But I just wanted it on the record.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: It's a way of that commitment, but we'll certainly take that back.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how people in custody are identified for mental health services upon entry. Jeanette Merrill says all new admissions can be referred to CHS mental health, evaluated for level of care, and then housed in appropriate units such as PACE, MO, or STEP.
chapters.title: Chair asks how DOC identifies people needing mental health services

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Now we can get into it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Let's start with mental health care and specialized housing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How does DOC currently identify people in custody who need mental health services when they enter the jail system?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So I think we can actually take that one, CHS.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So as referenced in Dr.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: Otanachar's testimony, so everyone who goes through the new admission process at Rikers can be referred to the mental health service depending on their mental health needs.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: They conducted an evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: They're assessing the level of care that the individual will require when on Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And that can mean specialized housing units.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: We referenced PACE, the mental observation units, and then our new form of housing, STEP.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: And then that information is shared with the department to transfer the individual into the appropriate housing unit.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks for the current mental observation census. Otonichar says there are 629 patients across 17 MO units.
chapters.title: Chair asks how many people are housed in mental observation units

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many people are currently housed in mental observation units?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So for mental observation units, the current census is 629 patients, and that's across 17 units.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Oh, sure.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: 629 patients across 17 MO units.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers recounts prior testimony on CAPS and mental observation beds. Otonichar says one CAPS unit is operating, and Assistant Chief Caputo confirms 23 people are currently housed there.
chapters.title: Chair asks about CAPS units and current census

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In September 2022, CHS testified that there were two CAPS units with five people housing CAPS at the time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In October 2023, DOC testified that there were 830 mental observation beds consisting of

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: 334 paste beds and 496 mental observation beds.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: CAPS was not separately identified in that breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are there currently any CAPS units operating?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: There's one CAPS unit in operation.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I believe 21 or 23 individuals are currently housed there.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: There's 23 people currently in CAPS.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: There's one CAPS unit currently in operation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how DOC ensures people receive medication at scheduled times. Boyd cites ongoing collaboration with CHS and medication windows or housing-unit distribution, while Otonichar says therapeutic housing units can provide medication on site.
chapters.title: Chair questions medication access and continuity

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What steps is DOC taking to ensure a person in their custody has consistent access to their medication at the times they're supposed to take such medication?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Well, I mean, that's continued collaboration with CHS.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Anyone that's produced that requires access to medication is produced to the appropriate medication windows or, you know, distributed medication in the housing unit.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I mean, we have frequent ongoing conversations at the exec level, but also at the local level in each jail.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: All of the wardens have conversations with the CHS staff directly on site to ensure that that continuity of care and access to medication is being afforded.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And I'll just add, one of the benefits of the therapeutic housing units is that medication can be provided on site.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So those are units where mental health professionals, actually they have offices, they're engaging directly with patients there, particularly on PACE unit.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: If a patient wasn't able to receive medication from a pharmacy technician earlier in the day, the nursing staff may be able to engage with them better later that day so they don't miss the dose.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you both.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many people have transferred to Bellevue's outposted therapeutic health unit since opening. Otonichar says the current census is 81, with 18 in the PACE unit, and discusses plans for Woodhull and North Central Bronx units.
chapters.title: Chair questions Bellevue outposted therapeutic unit capacity and expansion

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Regarding the outposted therapeutic health units,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many people have been transferred from Rikers to the Bellevue Outposted Therapeutic Health Unit since it opened?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So I don't have the total number transferred.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I can tell you the current census is 81 patients, and 18 of those patients are on the PACE unit, which, as mentioned earlier,

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: the PACE unit at the Bellevue Outposted unit is for individuals who have comorbid psychological and medical complexities.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Most of the beds at Bellevue Outposted are for people who have medical complexities, and there are 63 patients for those.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So all 104 bids are not operational right now.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: They're operational, but they aren't currently filled.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So in terms of bed capacity, that would differ from ideal clinical capacity.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We have to take into account things like patients'acuity, need, the therapeutic milieu of the unit.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So we wouldn't necessarily want every bed to be filled at every moment.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: That said, I believe Bellevue Outposted is holding some beds for patients who are currently hospitalized, knowing that they'll need to be returned to the unit.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So with that in mind, are there any plans to expand the number of beds at Bellevue beyond the current capacity?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Not at Bellevue.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: That unit has 104 beds, but we are in the process of opening two additional units.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We are in the procurement phase for the construction of the outposted unit at Woodhull.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We hope to be in the procurement stage soon for North Central Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And those two units, unlike the Bellevue unit, will be focused more on patients with significant mental health needs, particularly Woodhull,

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: as they may have some comorbid medical or substance use needs, but it'll primarily be psychological concerns.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so NADA is in procurement.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Once it goes from the...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I imagine it goes into design.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We've been working on design, so we're hoping to start construction of the actual outposted units early next year,

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: and then working towards 2029 opening dates for both units, although there's interest throughout the administration in expediting that, so we are looking for opportunities to move out that timeline.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers raises the August 19 death of Christopher Rodriguez at Bellevue and asks about the cause. Boyd says the cause is pending investigation and autopsy, and the chair presses on why autopsies for earlier deaths remain unresolved.
chapters.title: Chair questions Christopher Rodriguez death and autopsy delays

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: On August 19th, Christopher Rodriguez died while being housed at Bellevue Hospital.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When he was found, he was in a quote-unquote medical distress state before being pronounced dead at 8.39 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Rodriguez was the sixth death of a person in the department's custody this year.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do we know what the cause of his death was?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: At this time, we don't, but I will echo Commissioner Richard's statement and extend our condolences to Mr.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Rodriguez's family.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Our hearts go out to them, but at this time, it is pending investigation, and that final determination regarding the medical autopsy is still pending.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just segueing real quick, just on the autopsies, because we're, I think, up to eight deaths now for this year.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And every time I get a call, I ask about the previous deaths in terms of the status of the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I'm just curious as to why it's taken so long, because even with the toxology reports, I understand they take a little bit longer in time, but...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I think the earliest death may have been like February, March, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And we still don't even know the cause of death for that person.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And we're now in September.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But if a regular New Yorker needed to go through the medical examiner, have an autopsy and a toxology report, we would have had the results by now.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So what is the delay with the department for these results?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Well, that determination regarding how somebody succumbed to whatever happened to them is through the medical examiner's office.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so it can take a few months before we receive the final determination.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: When we understand that, you know, those final determinations can bring the family members closure and we'll support them throughout this process to make sure they know who to contact.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I'm going to have to defer to the OCME regarding their timelines to make that final determination.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: That's not something that the department looks into.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We rely on our partners to share that information.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So the department doesn't ask why it's taken so long or what the timeline is?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I mean, we will engage with them, certainly.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I mean, we've had a longstanding partner with OCME, but, you know, they...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because it's taken longer than the average New Yorker, and you all are an agency.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: A sister agency.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I would imagine you would be able to get the information sooner.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I mean, we can certainly circle back and we can have those conversations with them.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: You know, they're looking at this from the citywide lens as well.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: But we're open to have those conversations to see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Absolutely.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks when Rodriguez went into distress and what policies are being reviewed. Otonichar cites patient privacy and ongoing joint assessment review, while Boyd says the State Attorney General's Office, DOI, and Board of Correction are investigating.
chapters.title: Chair asks about Rodriguez distress timeline, JAR review, and investigating agencies

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do you know when he went into distress?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We know when he passed, but do we know approximately the time he went into distress?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So we wouldn't be able to speak about any particular patient case here.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I will say, you know, the department works with all of the various oversight bodies, reports the death.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We do our own processes internally, including a joint assessment review, a JAR, that's joint with the department.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We review under our own mortality and morbidity review committees, the New York City Board of Directors, Health and Hospitals Board of Directors also reviews.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: But because of patient privacy concerns I'm not able to discuss publicly.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you share what was done?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Once he was found in distress.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I think those conversations are still ongoing with the department and under investigation.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I will say there is a Board of Correction report that ultimately will come out and that will provide more information.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When will that report be out?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I would defer to BOC, Board of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are any policies at Bellevue being evaluated as a result of Mr.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Rodriguez's death?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Part of the JAR, the Joint Assessment and Review, is examining any policies, procedures that may have played a role.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I think it's, again, premature now, but that could be a corrective action following a patient death.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And to your point with the JAR, which people or what entities are involved in investigating Mr.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Rodriguez's death?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: For investigation, I mean.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the State Attorney General's Office, the Department of Investigation, as well as the Board of Correction.

chapters.title: Chair closes vote; Introduction 246A passes 6-0

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: With that, the vote has been closed.
