chapters.summary: Chair Brooks-Powers resumes the hearing and yields to Council Member Mercedes Narcisse. Narcisse asks how many mental health appointments were missed due to DOC non-production. Boyd says about 10% of over 60,000 mental health appointments this year were missed for reasons including no escort, alarms, or lockdowns.
chapters.title: Narcisse questions missed mental health appointments and non-production

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: All right, we'll now continue the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I am going to yield my questions for the moment and move to member questions, starting with Councilmember Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I have to start by saying thank you, Madam Chair, for always being present and on point.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have, I mean,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: question about how mental health is affecting people that's not even in incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So having like kids, and I'm so happy that you're on board with us, with the children, because we have to be mindful of the folks that's not present in the background.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you for all your leadership.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We hear that routine medical appointment, right, often missed.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is the same thing happening with mental health appointments?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How many were missed in the last fiscal year because DOC did not produce the patients and what share of all the scheduled mental health appointments?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is that.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Specific to mental health appointments.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: So I have for a calendar year to date, so the first eight months of this year, there was over 60,000 mental health appointments.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: About 10% of those appointments were due to non-production that could have been related to either no escort or an alarm, a TSO, or lockdown.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so that's a really small percentage when you compare it to the total amount of scheduled appointments.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so, again, we do prioritize medical appointments in the jails.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: That is a daily, ongoing conversation every day, 24-7, right?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so if someone missed their medical appointment in the morning, DOC staff in that particular facility is going to be working with CHS staff to see if they can produce them the same day.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so there's always ongoing conversation to make sure we're giving people access to the care that they need, and that's an ongoing partnership we have with CHS.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so there are things we're going to internally do, you know, to figure out how we can make this process more efficient, but we're moving in the right direction when we strive to make sure people are produced to their clinic appointment.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In all honesty, I can say it's progress because it's only 10%, but the 10% still matter.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So, and I'm happy to hear that you're going to make every effort because every appointment, especially when it comes to mental health.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what share of people leave with a discharge plan, medication supply, and community appointment, and how follow-up is tracked. Otonichar describes Medicaid enrollment, prescriptions, reentry resources, and voluntary services. Narcisse says the voluntary nature concerns her given community mental health needs.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about discharge plans, medication, and community follow-up

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What share of people live with the discharge plan, a medication supply, and a scheduled appointment in the community?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How are you tracking whether they're...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: actually make that appointment.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We spoke back and forth about that before.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are we doing the follow-up?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So I guess to start, we provide core reentry services to every person in custody.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Crucially, that is ensuring that they have Medicaid access on their release.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So we're checking whether they came in with coverage.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: If they did not, then we can help them apply.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We're also sending prescriptions to the pharmacy of their choice on their release.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We're connecting them or referring them to the various services Dr.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Otanachar referenced in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We have the community reentry network.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We have the port primary care practices at Bellevue and Kings.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We have a port line that individuals can call.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And then patients who are enrolled in the mental health service can also leave Rikers with meds in hand.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I will say all of our services in the jails as well as any community referrals are all voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So we aren't necessarily tracking or ensuring, but we are trying to remove as many barriers as possible so that if someone wants to access that care in the community, they're able to.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The voluntary part bothers me because when a lot of folks end up in the community, and especially the black and brown communities, now more than ever, you see now young folks walking around with...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: serious mental health problem, and there is no place to go and no community arrangement, I think we have to make maximum effort to make sure those populations that are coming from incarceration are being addressed.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about people without medical coverage or paperwork, including TPS recipients. Otonichar says about 85% have Medicaid on release and that Health and Hospitals provides care regardless of ability to pay.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about uninsured detainees and Medicaid coverage

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now, another question I'd be remiss not to ask, how about those folks that don't have no medical coverage and that on the TPS or different reason, they don't have no paperwork and they're not getting insurance in the outside world?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are you making maximum effort to refer them to a place where they can get support?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So about 85% of people in custody, we estimate, will have Medicaid coverage on their release, either because we've helped enroll them or they're previously enrolled.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I think that's where we're incredibly fortunate to have New York City Health and Hospitals in our city because the system provides care to everyone, regardless of their ability to pay.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And that is something that individuals can certainly call Portline, which is the peer staff reentry line, to help get connected there, or they can go into CRAN to get connected.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether therapy is offered in multiple languages. Otonichar says CHS adheres to community standards and uses interpreter services in person or by phone or video. Narcisse also flags future budget questions on psychiatric care.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks how interpretation is handled in therapy

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Chair, may I ask a quick question?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How is interpretation handled in a therapy session?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are sessions offered in multiple languages?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So we adhere to the community standards of care.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Of course, if somebody is not a native English speaker, it's of paramount importance that we offer services in the language of their preference.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And typically we do use interpreter services.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: for that either in person or through a telephone or video system.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Me and my chair are going, but I'm going to circle back.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But the budget is interesting for me because I want to know how much money is being allocated when it comes to psychiatric.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

chapters.summary: Council Member Frank Morano asks Otonichar whether housing someone with mental illness in general population means it is clinically best or simply the best available. Otonichar says patients are continuously assessed and that PACE waitlist currently includes 24 patients needing higher care.
chapters.title: Morano questions whether general population is clinically appropriate

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We're going to go to Councilmember Marano.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'd love to begin with Dr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Otonashar.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You testified that most people with mental health needs are appropriately housed in general population.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I want to be very precise about the word appropriately.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When CHS says someone is appropriately housed in general population, does that mean CHS believes general population is the clinically best placement?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Or can it mean it's simply the best placement currently available?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So we continuously assess throughout an individual's incarceration what their clinical needs are, how closely they need to be monitored.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Similar to the community standard, patients who are able to function higher and less in distress are able to be brought to their appointment similar to the way you and I would go to an outpatient clinic.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: For those individuals who are more vulnerable, who benefit from closer monitoring, who benefit from

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: greater support, we would transfer those patients onto a therapeutic housing unit until those needs are stabilized.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And we often will keep them there indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So specifically, among people with serious mental illness who are currently in general population, how many would be in a more therapeutic setting if every clinically appropriate bed were available today?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Can you rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So among people with serious mental illness who are currently in general population,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: how many would be in a more therapeutic setting if every clinically appropriate bed were available today?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We consistently do assess the needs and assign patients to whatever level of care is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Currently, all patients who require a particular level of care are transferred to that level of care.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So what we have is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Particularly understanding.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I think another way of thinking about it, there's currently 24 patients who are waiting placement on a PACE unit, so they do require a higher level of care.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We had an influx of hospital returns, and so those individuals are being closely monitored on MO, but they do require PACE.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: But I do think it's a common misconception that anyone who has a serious mental illness requires a residential treatment level of care.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So GP is...

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Clinically appropriate.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether unmet CHS recommendations for higher care are tracked and published. Boyd says placement concerns are discussed with CHS, and Caputo says CHS knows bed availability when making recommendations and that DOC does not reject higher-care placements.
chapters.title: Morano asks Boyd about unmet clinical recommendations and PACE waits

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner Boyd, obviously you're responsible for quality assurance and compliance.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If CHS recommends a higher level of care and Department of Corrections can't provide the bed, is that recorded somewhere as an unmet clinical recommendation?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And if it is, do you publish that number?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I think if there is a concern regarding the placement, then that's where we'll have that conversation.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: If it's a concern about the safety of individuals where the requested placement for these individuals should go to, then we're having that conversation with CHS to see if they could be placed somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so if there's really serious concerns about...

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: A challenging detainee who might need to be placed in PACE or another unit, and we think they might be a threat to the safety of other folks in that particular housing unit, then that's a conversation with CHS to see if they could be placed somewhere else and still receive

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: the same level of care.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think it does in part.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I guess what I'm wondering is if there's specific data available about people that are being recommended for a higher level of care when we don't have the resources for that bed.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I'm wondering what that number is.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: So, good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: I'm Joseph Caputo.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: I'm the Assistant Chief of the Criminal Justice Bureau on Facility Operations.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: So, in reference to your question, we are partners with CHS.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: CHS is aware of the number of beds that are available when they make the placement recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: So, like it was alluded to as far as the PACE unit, that there is individuals that they're tracking based upon space and ensuring that they meet their clinical needs while they're pending that bed.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: We are not.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: rejecting people that need a higher level of care in the mental health, especially in that mental health population aspect of things.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: And we're partners with CHS in making the affecting the placements.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: And they're aware of the number of beds when they make those recommendations.

chapters.summary: Morano notes the city has thousands more people in custody than the 4,160 beds planned for borough-based jails. He worries the city may exacerbate mental health housing problems under new capacity. He yields back with time expired.
chapters.title: Morano raises borough-based jail capacity concerns

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So just so for context, the reason why I'm asking is, as you know far better than I do, the city currently has thousands more people in custody than the 4,160 beds

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: planned for the borough-based jail system.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And the city itself says those new facilities are supposed to provide appropriate housing for people with medical and mental health needs.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I'm just wondering if we're not already there, if we're going to be exacerbating the problem under the new capacity.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I know my time's up.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Cabán asks why transgender people are sent to gender-misaligned facilities and why nearly half of transfer requests are denied. Deputy Commissioner Nell Colon cites PREA standards and case-by-case determinations, saying DOC tries to align housing once aware of a person's preference.
chapters.title: Cabán questions gender misaligned intake and denials of gender-aligned housing

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next, Councilmember McCubbon.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm out of breath, but I got back in time.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm going to start with questions about my bill.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The TGNC-NBI task force, they recommended that gender-aligned housing be the presumptive placement unless the individual incarcerated requests otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So the question is, why are transgender people being sent to gender misaligned facilities upon intake?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And why is DOC denying nearly half of all applications of requests for transfers to gender aligned facilities?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that's based on y'all's own data.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: That's the information we're getting from you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I'll start there.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Nell Colon.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Commissioner of Programs and Community Partnerships.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And just for context, within the Division of Programs and Community Partnerships, the LGBTQ Affairs Unit is housed.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And so just to speak to this, I mean, when considering placement, the department does, one of the primary focuses is

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: complying with the national PRIA standards.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Each determination is made on a case-by-case basis, but I think to what you just indicated is that, yes, there are times where

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: somebody may have an indication and when they're transported from court to a site, it may not be the right site, but once we become aware,

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: and a conversation happens and a person is able to state their preference based on their gender identity, we make our best attempt to make sure that they're in a gender-aligned facility.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But at this point, half of those applications are, more than half are being denied.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And to your point about the PRIA guidelines, we had a hearing on this last term, and specifically we had conversations about how

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Priya is obviously meant to protect people, but it is misinterpreted by folks in the DOC and outside in ways that actually disproportionately harm transgendered individuals.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that's something that needs to be reassessed.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that's also a reason why this task force is so incredibly important.

chapters.summary: Cabán asks what specific criteria accounted for 106 denials out of 231 gender-aligned housing applications. Colon lists factors including stated gender identity, security concerns, mental health, and classification, but says she does not have a breakdown of gender-based violence findings.
chapters.title: Cabán presses DOC on criteria for 106 gender-aligned housing denials

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Can you talk about the specific criteria that accounted for the 106 denials?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: out of the 231 applications for gender-aligned housing?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yes, so when a placement decision is being made, there's a number of factors that are considered.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: One is the individual's stated gender identity, as well as their preferred placement, SCU, gender-aligned housing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: With that, there's also overriding security and management concerns that are factored in.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, just to interrupt, because I have limited time.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: What specific criteria accounted for the denials?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We're aware of what the factors are, but which factors accounted for the denials, 106 denials?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Well, I think that that's what all of these factors are.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Put in place on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So if we're talking about, let's say, the overriding security and management concerns, pre-screening information, mental health or medical concerns, classification, all of these things may be factors based on somebody's housing place.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So of the 106 denials then, how many involve a finding that the individual presented a current danger of committing gender-based violence, which is the standard recommended by the task force?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yes, I actually specifically don't have the gender-based violence indicator number for you, so I just want to be transparent.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Can you get it?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then if DOC relied on other grounds for denying the applications, other grounds outside of the current danger for committing gender-based violence,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm assuming you don't have a breakdown of what those grounds were.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: In the context of what we have to give you today.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I would also ask for those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I think it's really important to get a sense of, you know, what other factors are serving as the basis for denying placement of cisgender people in gender-aligned facilities.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I mean...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The DOC is essentially continuing to use criteria that's inconsistent with the task force's recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And obviously when you provide that information, you know, appropriately redacted, but we want to see it.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: From there,

chapters.summary: Cabán asks whether DOC implemented the task force recommendation for automatic independent review of housing denials within three business days. Colon says DOC has not implemented that specific recommendation but policies are under review under the remediation manager and current leadership.
chapters.title: Cabán asks why DOC has not implemented independent review of housing denials

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to ask why DOC hasn't implemented the task force's recommendation for automatic independent review of housing denials.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The task force recommended that every denial of gender-aligned housing should be supported by a detailed written decision, identifying the evidence relied on, and receive automatic independent review within three business days by officials who weren't involved in the original decision.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Have you implemented that recommendation?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: At this time, we have not implemented that specific recommendation, but I do know, I just want to put this on the record, that our policy is under review.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And actually, many of our policies are under review, particularly now that we're under a remediation manager along with our current leadership.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And so all of our policies are being thoroughly...

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Reviewed to make sure that we're taking in these.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Chair, because I'm going to leave to chair another hearing, can I have a couple extra minutes?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to give you two extra because they said they don't have a problem with it.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I just want to say I'm glad that it's being reviewed.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I hope that you take those recommendations to heart and especially making sure that it's the reconsideration process is not merely allowing an individual to request reconsideration, but that it's an automatic independent review.

chapters.summary: Cabán says the number of people in DOC custody with serious mental illness has increased over 80% since 2022. She asks how that affects quality care, whether ACT or IMT referrals are confirmed, and how CHS collaborates with other agencies.
chapters.title: Cabán questions 80% rise in serious mental illness and ACT/IMT placements

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: My other questions, and I know that the chair is going to do a phenomenal job picking up on these mental health questions, but the number of people in DOC custody with serious mental health illness, it's increased by over 80% since 2022.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's a much steeper increase than the general population.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: that we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so my questions are, how does this increase affect your ability to provide quality care for people in custody, which I know that my colleague, Councilmember Rano, alluded to.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And when you refer, I'm just asking them in succession, when you refer somebody to ACT or IMT, do you confirm if and when they have been placed and how, in your experience, how long does it take?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: To assign somebody to a team.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then I'm going to close that out and finish by just saying that with that serious mental illness increase by over 80%, it speaks to a larger problem outside of corrections.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You don't control who comes into your care, and I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But what are you guys doing?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Doing to, with other agencies, to ring the bell on this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: These are people who are living with serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: They should not be criminalized for said mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that means that there's a deep, deep failure in the continuum of care outside of corrections.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so what does that work in collaboration look like?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Those are the three questions.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you for indulging me, Chair.

chapters.summary: Otonichar says the serious mental illness rate is about 22%, up from prior years, and that CHS uses therapeutic units and clinic appointments while recognizing jail is not conducive to mental health. Ellie Epstein describes SPOA referrals and limits in tracking community placements after release.
chapters.title: CHS answers on SMI care, SPOA referrals, and reentry tracking

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Okay, so I think to start, care for the SMI population, we have seen an increase, as we referenced.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: It's about 22% currently.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: When we look back in prior years, range from about 16% to 20% in recent years.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And part of ensuring we meet their needs does involve these assessments that we do and then constantly evaluating based on referrals to the mental health service.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: That said, we do recognize we have some very

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: psychologically complex patients in our care.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We do have the ability to refer those individuals to Bellevue or Elmhurst for potential hospitalization as needed.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: But generally speaking, we're through the therapeutic units and then clinic appointments, we're able to address their needs while they're with us.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: But that's not to say that the jail environment is in any way conducive to mental health.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: In terms of work that we do with outside partners.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So we do, based on clinical criteria, refer individuals to the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene's single point of access, SPOA.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We're not the only ones making those referrals.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: The shelter system, health and hospitals, also refers individuals.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And then they are making those determinations for appropriateness and acceptance into things like intensive mobile treatment teams, the forensic assertive community treatment.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So they would be the best position to speak to sort of numbers.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: But we otherwise work with our partners in DSS HRA for housing applications.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So everyone who is homeless in our care and has serious mental illness and is interested, we will help them complete a 2010E supportive housing application.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And then we do more broadly work through our clinical court advocacy team.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: They can serve as a...

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Resource to Defense Bar, we can write clinical condition letters.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Those tend to skew more for the medically complex.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And then we work on the jail population review.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We're a partner in providing with consent patient information around health and mental health to help get people out of jail.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Which place?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Of the number of referrals we're making?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We would have a number of referrals in terms of placement.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I think the department would be best, but if my colleague wants to speak more directly.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: If you can make the response tight, we're going to pivot to Councilmember Brewer next.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: I'm Ellie Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: I lead our reentry and transition services for Correctional Health Services.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: So as you're aware, the vast majority of our patients are pretrial detainees.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: When they receive a SPOA assignment while they are still in our care, we're obviously tracking that and facilitating connection to the team.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: When folks are released from custody, we notify DOHMH if they have not yet been assigned so that they're aware of the release.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: But no, we recognize that when patients leave our care and leave custody, they often don't want to have continued contact with our system.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: So we will outreach, but we really defer to DOHMH to make those connections and to be tracking the longer-term placements.

chapters.summary: Council Member Gale Brewer asks whether Bellevue's 104 beds are all medical and how many mentally ill patients are homeless. Otonichar explains the PACE unit at Bellevue serves comorbid psychiatric and medical needs and says 31% of homeless patients have serious mental illness.
chapters.title: Brewer questions Bellevue's medical focus and homelessness among mentally ill

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Two questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One is, maybe I misunderstood Bellevue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've been to the new wonderful facility twice, I think, with Dr.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Katz.

utterances.text: There are 104 beds.

utterances.text: I thought they were 100% medical.

utterances.text: Is that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what he told me.

utterances.text: No, that's true.

utterances.text: Everyone there has complex medical needs.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: It's just the PACE unit is for individuals who have those medical needs as well as significant psychiatric needs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, so there is a medical component to it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Second, how many people do you know within the categorized as mental illness are also homeless so that when they are released, they're going back to, I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Yeah, so we actually do have that analysis from January through June of this year.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: 31% of our homeless patients also have serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So 31% would be homeless and mentally ill is what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Yes, and I will say the way we categorize homelessness, it's self-reported by patients, whether they didn't have housing before they entered or likely to be unhoused on release.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, that's a pretty high percentage, 31%.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: It's just higher than the general population.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So about 28% of people on Rikers right now.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So when they get released, they're going somewhere.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So that means that medication may not be easy to obtain.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: prescription to the pharmacy of their choice and then if they're enrolled they can also leave with medication maybe my colleague wants to no but i know this population they they don't go where they're supposed to go

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: yeah they do lead yes complicated lives they don't we do prescribe walking medications for people to take with them as well

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: So individuals who receive mental health treatment upon their release from custody, if they're being released from Rikers Island, will come into the clinic and we make available, as my colleague mentioned, we'll make available physical medication so they can leave with some medication in hand.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: We also have a variety of different resources.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: To your point, our port line, which is the peer-staffed hotline, we often have patients or providers working with those patients call in and we reroute prescriptions.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: So, for example, if they are no longer able to get to the pharmacy that originally made sense, we also proactively call patients where we have contact information to remind them about the pharmacy where those prescriptions were sent.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about recidivism rates for people in mental health programs. Epstein says CHS does not track recidivism as a health care service, though many patients return, and Otonichar says CHS could look into available data.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about recidivism among mentally ill people returning to Rikers

utterances.text: I mean, I just know how folks are.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two is, do you have any sense of those recidivism who have been in your mental health programs who may or may not be homeless?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But what is the recidivism rate for those who have been at Rikers, obviously awaiting something, and who are returning who are mentally, you consider mentally ill?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have any sense of that?

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: So we're not tracking recidivism as the health care service.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: We do know that many of our patients do return.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We know that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We don't have any sense of those that are mentally ill.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: In terms of analysis, we could look into what we have, other agencies may have data on returns.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, that's what the issue is out there in the community.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what's said, whether it's true or not.

Epstein says CHS has made recruitment and retention efforts and has only one vacancy in that area, though pretrial detention makes discharge planning difficult.
chapters.title: Brewer questions social worker staffing and discharge planning compliance

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In terms of Brad H., I know that the most recent compliance report noted that CHS hired three more social workers, up to 90%.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So have you had any more social workers hired?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have any sense of recruitment?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because the issue for me is the discharge plan staff categories.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It should be 100%.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I guess I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm still concerned about those that are leaving having enough support.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I guess you've never quite been in compliance with this discharge planning.

utterances.text: Can you bring us up to date on staffing, discharge planning, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: We know the quality of our discharge planning service is dependent upon those staff.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: Our vacancy rate, I'd have to double check, but I believe we only have one posting, I think, at the moment.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: So we are very close to full staffing.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: Again, much of the challenge is that most of our patients are pretrial detainees, and so we don't have an expected discharge date, which really makes planning and being able to put together a solid plan extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: And I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: What was the other part of your question?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, well, you mostly did.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I guess the issue, that's enough to answer.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how long it takes between a mental health referral and initial clinical evaluation. Otonichar says in July about 1,800 intakes occurred, roughly 1,000 were referred to mental health, and 95% were seen within 72 hours; stat referrals are scheduled within 24 hours.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about referral-to-evaluation time and Bellevue clinic use

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But my other question is, what's the average time between a mental health referral?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: and the person's initial clinical evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And it must have, when I go, I'm no expert, obviously, but it doesn't seem like there's a lot of services.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A lot of mental illness, maybe just because that's the day that I'm there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: James and Chelsea know that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But it doesn't seem like it's under control.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I guess my question is also in terms of the medical clinics on site at Bellevue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many on them are?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many appointments are for mentally ill on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How are those clinics used?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: When I was there, nobody was at the clinic.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I can start with the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So in terms of how long it takes, so looking at July data from this year, we completed about 1,800 intakes.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Of that, about 1,000 individuals were referred to mental health, and 95% of them were seen within 72 hours.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Otherwise, we can make stat referrals in general to mental health service, which is trying to see people within or schedule people within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: More routine appointments will be scheduled within 72 hours.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: In terms of the Bellevue Clinic, because that is a therapeutic unit and individuals and staff are on site, our utilization rates are higher.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We can follow up with you on any specifics related to mental health.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, I'll just leave it that this is the biggest problem in the city right now, number one.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so it needs even more attention than this wonderful chair is doing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I know you're kind of saying everything's okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's not okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's not okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so, I mean, obviously more follow-up, but this...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Out on the street, a lot of your focus, people who have been at Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you just need to do a lot more.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: No, I understand.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: And I think your point about homelessness is a good one.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Yeah, they're not going to take that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're not going to any pharmacy of their choice.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They don't know what the hell that is.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's hard to, you know, they're out.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a few questions, and then I'm going to you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Oh, no, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Councilmember Salam has not gone.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Go ahead.

chapters.summary: Council Member Yusef Salaam asks how much of the 40% unseen mental health appointment rate is refusal, officer non-production, or lock-ins, and asks about Bellevue's rate. Boyd says he lacks granular data but can follow up on missed appointments.
chapters.title: Salaam asks about missed appointment causes and Bellevue's 81% rate

utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.text: About 40% of scheduled mental health appointments go unseen.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: How much of that is refusal?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: How much is officers not bringing people to the clinic?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: How much is lock-ins?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And what explains the gap with Bellevue's early 81% rate?

utterances.text: Which point in time?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: I guess since the open?

utterances.text: Specific to Bellevue Hospital, the OTXB?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: The prison, yes.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I don't have that granular data, but we can certainly follow up on any missed medical appointments.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I don't know if there's anything else you want to add, but I mean, I don't know if you visited, but, you know, it's the whole kind of intent of this space is to make sure that there are direct access to services, which is on site on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: But however, we can follow up on that data in a follow up.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Salaam asks how many yearly reports the TGNC-NBI task force has issued and whether Intro 133 would extend anything beyond the fifth report. Colon says the task force issued one large report in 2022 and continues to meet quarterly even though the original local law timeframe ended.
chapters.title: Salaam asks about task force reports and what Intro 133 extends

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: For intro 133, how many yearly reports has the task force issued?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: If the fifth is already out, does this bill extend anything?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So the task force issued a very large report in 2022.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: The department responded to it.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: It was one report.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And at this time, the task force still continues to meet regularly on a quarterly basis, although technically the timeframe for the original task force based on the original local law ceased, but we continue to participate in the task force meetings on a quarterly basis.

chapters.summary: Salaam asks who would deliver and fund mental health services for children visiting incarcerated individuals if DOC is not a healthcare provider. Colon says DOC does not provide clinical treatment and lists existing partnerships, but says the city does not yet know which agency or funding source would be best.
chapters.title: Salaam asks who would deliver and fund Intro 453 services

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: For intro 453, who would actually deliver these services and how would it be funded since DOC is not a healthcare provider?

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So we greatly support making sure that

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: children and young people visiting family members and loved ones and parents do receive the support and referrals that they need.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I think part of this bill, so DOC, as you mentioned, we currently do not provide mental health clinical treatment.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: So DOC staff providing it would not be the answer in this scenario.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I don't think that we at this time have an exact determination of who would be best suited to provide that treatment.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: We do have multiple partners that we actually work with right now on smaller scale initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I can share some of those.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: First and foremost, we have a partnership at the Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice with the Visiting and Family Assistance Program that partners with our children and the Osborne Association.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: with a small subgroup of participants and parents that get and receive additional support for their children.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: We also participate with the Administration of Children's Services, ACS, who has the longstanding CHIP program, I mean decades longstanding CHIP program that provides support to children, but that's specific to those who might be in the foster care system.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: We recently started a partnership with the New York City Public Schools, where we're working with their counselors and caseworkers at the New York City Public Schools in a televisit pilot with parents who are also incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And a core component of that is that the parents are going through a parenthood program simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And then last, one of our most successful parenthood programs that we've been working with is in partnership with DYCD.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And that partnership has grew from one pilot to multiple facility sites now.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And that parenthood program also offers support.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: Through family days and activities intended to improve family, like parent-child bonding.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: And then we have obviously partnered with the Children's Museum of Manhattan and the Brooklyn Children's Museum to provide off-site visits.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: We've worked with the Children's Museum of Manhattan to improve our visit spaces, but I think when we

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: think more globally about partnerships and who would be that primary person for the referrals for clinical mental health treatment.

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: I don't know if we at this time know exactly who that would be or where that funding would come from and how much funding would be necessary to make sure that the right provider or the right age

utterances.speaker: Nell Colon
utterances.text: is providing that level of treatment and services that is greatly needed for children.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Definitely agree.
