chapters.summary: Morano relays a question from Council Member Narcisse about vacant mental health clinician positions. Otonichar says CHS has 244 FTEs in mental health and 33 vacancies, and that recruitment is challenging in carceral settings.
chapters.title: Morano asks about vacant mental health clinician positions

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have one quick question from my colleague, Councilmember Narcisse, who had to run, and then a couple quick questions of my own.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: She asks, how many budgeted mental health clinician positions are vacant right now, psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, and nurses?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And knowing Councilmember Narcisse as we do, this is usually the portion where she would mention that she herself is a nurse.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I'll mention that on her behalf.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So we currently have 244 FTEs in the mental health service and 33 vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I will note we have really stepped up our recruitment efforts in mental health.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: It is an incredibly sought-after profession generally, and carceral mental health care is particularly challenging, and then Rikers itself has unique challenges as well.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: But they do a phenomenal job meeting the needs.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: With the current staffing.

chapters.summary: Morano asks Boyd what single metric shows whether access is improving. Boyd cites production data and the clinic production dashboard, an electronic system being piloted at two facilities to track scheduled, unscheduled, and walk-in appointments in real time.
chapters.title: Morano asks Boyd for key access metric and clinic production dashboard

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Returning to Deputy Commissioner Boyd, you indicated that the department is laser focused on improving access to mental health services, and I think that's something that we're all appreciative of and grateful for.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What's the single most important metric that you use to determine whether access is actually improving?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Well, I think in my kind of short tenure overseeing this portfolio, I have been laser focused on the data regarding production.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And I want to improve that data, improve transparency within the department.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Most of the department's processes is a reliance on paper.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And that's why I've been advancing the clinic production dashboard, which I mentioned at previous hearings is an electronic database that the department is going to use to track the universe of clinic appointments, whether it's scheduled, unscheduled, and walk-ins.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And I think that process is going to strengthen coordination with CHS and enhance production so we can communicate and track production in real time.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: To see if the person was moved from the housing area to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And I can look up on a dashboard and see if that actual person was produced as opposed to relying on paper, which somebody has to bring to you.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so, you know, it's in progress.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We rolled it out at two facilities.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: It's still in the pilot phase.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: But we're really excited about that because that is the path forward.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: That is a legacy project.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So since you specifically cited the clinic production dashboard as one of the department's modernization projects,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: does that dashboard distinguish between a patient who refuses an appointment and a patient who wants the appointment but the Department of Correction fails to produce?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: It does track, well, departmental policy is that if someone refuses to be produced to a clinic appointment, is that we track it on body one camera.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so if an escort officer is going to the housing area and the person in custody says, I don't want to go, they are to tap their body-worn camera and record that encounter.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I have to go back to see how do we document that into the clinic production dashboard.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I don't think we're there yet, but it's something we can definitely consider.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether the dashboard distinguishes patient refusals from DOC failure to produce. Boyd says refusals are recorded on body-worn camera and about 61% of all missed appointments were related to patient refusals, while Caputo says refusals are codified separately from court or other service absences.
chapters.title: Morano asks how missed appointments distinguish refusals from DOC failures

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do we know, for instance, what percentage of missed mental health appointments this year were attributable to refusals versus the department?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I don't think I have that broken out by refusals for mental health appointments, but for the universe of appointments, about 61%

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: were related to PIC refusals, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And if an appointment's recorded as a refusal, does anyone ever go back and verify that that individual actually refused and wasn't simply unavailable because DOC couldn't move them?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: So the way we codify the missed appointments, that category of refusal is one.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: If an individual was out to court or if he was at another service, those are all different categories that we codify that under.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: So it's not under the blanket of refusal if the individual was at a different service or out to court.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: We don't codify it that way.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: That's not a refusal.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers pivots to deadlocking and asks whether DOC can assure the council it no longer occurs. General Counsel James Conroy says DOI investigated prior allegations and did not find deadlocking as alleged, and that the administration is committed to proper documentation of lock-ins.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers questions whether deadlocking still occurs

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Pivot into deadlocking.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can the department assure the council that deadlocking is no longer occurring at all?

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: Sorry, good morning.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: James Conroy, General Counsel for the agency.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: Yes, that is something that we've represented and testified about in the past.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: The Department of Investigation, when this first was brought to our attention a couple of years ago, I guess at this point, at a Board of Correction hearing, it was referred to the Department of Investigation for...

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: Them to look into these allegations and they came back with a report or at least made a determination, although they issued a full report that they had not found instances of this as alleged at the Board of Correction hearing.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: So obviously the previous and this administration in particular is committed to ensuring that that is not going on and that any types of lock-ins are appropriately documented and appropriate in and of themselves.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether mental health units are regularly inspected for deadlocking and whether staff have received training or discipline. Conroy describes a tiered supervisory system, memoranda and training against unauthorized lock-ins, but says he does not know of any discipline and will follow up.
chapters.title: Chair asks about inspections, training, and discipline for deadlocking

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Still with deadlocking, are there regular inspections done of the mental health units around deadlocking?

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: I wouldn't categorize it as that specifically.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: Obviously, any of these types of lock-ins, we have an obligation and supervisor responsibility to ensure that any lock-in, if they are taking place, are documented, appropriate, and within guidelines.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: So that's a department-wide thing.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: I wouldn't necessarily limit that to the mental health spaces.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And who would be the...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The one doing that type of like regular inspection or check-in?

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: It's a tiered system, obviously, on a supervisory level.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: It starts with the supervisors at the housing area and then moving up into the facility and then, of course, going to our overarching executive staff on a uniform level.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Have correctional staff received any additional training or support to avoid them feeling that they need to resort to deadlocking?

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: At the time and continuing since that, this was raised as an issue, we've issued memoranda or teletypes and trainings to indicate that this is not an appropriate method to...

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: At all.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: It's not an approved practice whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: So I would say overall, yes.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: But again, I don't think it's necessarily focused or pointed to be specific.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: that word deadlocking.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: This is something that we do overarchingly for the entire department about what is the appropriate use in any circumstance of a lock-in or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Have any staff been disciplined for deadlocking?

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: I would have to get back.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: I don't know that I have that data.

utterances.speaker: James Conroy
utterances.text: You know, this goes back a couple of years for that investigation, but not to my knowledge, but we will certainly follow up.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether CHS disciplined employees for refusing to cooperate with the DOI investigation into deadlocking. Otonichar says he is not aware of any such discipline and will follow up, but says clinicians are expected to report barriers to patient access to supervisors.
chapters.title: Chair asks CHS about discipline for refusing DOI cooperation

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Um,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Did CHS discipline employees for refusing to cooperate with the Department of Investigations investigation?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I would need to follow up with you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Sorry, the question was whether we discipline staff related to deadlocking?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Yes, so I believe that DOI's investigation found that there was deadlocking done by CHS employees, that they were aware of it, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Okay, so I can't speak to...

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Any particular disciplinary actions, but I will say for the service, we did reinforce with staff that at any time one of our clinicians encounters a barrier to accessing a patient to

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: provide care, they are expected to report that to their supervisor.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Generally, that's dealt with on the local facility level in partnership with DOC, and then we can always escalate as needed for persistent or systemic issues.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many people in custody receive active mental health treatment, psychiatric medication, individual psychotherapy, and group therapy. Otonichar says about 4,018 people are under active mental health care, about 3,000 receive psychiatric medication, and about 1,100 are in therapeutic housing units.
chapters.title: Chair asks how many people receive active mental health treatment and medication

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: pivot into the mental health treatment.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many people currently in the department's custody are receiving active mental health treatment?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So the 61% of individuals who are enrolled in the mental health service represent individuals under active mental health care.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do you have a number, though?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Yes, that number.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: About 4,000.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many people are currently receiving psychiatric medication?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: About 3,000 individuals in custody.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many people are receiving individual psychotherapy?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So that would be a standard component of our mental health service, which, again, about 60% of individuals are under.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: The care of the mental health service.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Of course, what that looks like on an individual basis depends on patient need and interest.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many are receiving group therapy?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Similarly, so group therapy is available on the mental health units, of which about 14, or excuse me,

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: 1,100 patients are currently housed in a mental health therapeutic housing unit.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: That's not to say that every patient would choose to engage in group therapy because, again, all of our services are voluntary.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how CHS staff interface with mental observation units and how PACE units are staffed. Otonichar says MO units receive on-site services, regular rounding, groups, and medication, while PACE units have multidisciplinary teams including psychiatric providers, clinicians, nurses, treatment aides, and social workers.
chapters.title: Chair asks how CHS staffs mental observation and PACE units

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you explain how CHS staff interface with mental observation units?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Like how they do want to talk about.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: So our staff, like all of our mental health therapeutic housing units, provide services on site on the mental observation units.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We do regular rounding on those units to check in on all the patients, and we have a higher frequency of visits that we see patients for clinical services.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We also offer groups therapeutically directly on site on our mental observation units.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Medication as well as provided on site to those patients.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And can you explain how PACE units are staffed?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Yeah, so we have a very robust multidisciplinary team on our PACE units.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: That includes a psychiatric provider, mental health clinician, clinical supervisor, nursing staff, treatment aides, and discharge planning social workers who work together, meet regularly to talk about the care of each of the patients.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether CHS has hired more social workers since the last compliance report and why it has never been in full compliance with court-ordered discharge planning staffing. Epstein says CHS has only one vacancy, has improved salaries and recruitment, and faces challenges including difficult commutes.
chapters.title: Chair asks about social worker vacancies and discharge planning compliance

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The most recent Brad H.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Compliance report noted that CHS hired three additional social workers, bringing the social worker staffing rate up to 90%.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Has CHS hired any additional social workers since the last reporting period, June through December 2025?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Yes, that's what my colleague Ellie referenced.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I believe we only have one current vacancy, so we have staffed up.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is there an estimate to when that last position will be staffed?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I believe we're actively recruiting.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: I can let you know when it's filled.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Has CHS created any sort of retention and recruitment plan to increase the discharge plan staff categories, staffing rate to 100%?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: For that specific, I might call up my colleague.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: So we actually, over the last couple of years, have worked really hard to try and increase salaries to start engaging more with different school programs.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: We have an incredible internal program to support social workers who are pursuing their clinical hours and licensure.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: So we've done a lot of work to try and advertise the incredible opportunities available within our department, and we think that that's really making a difference.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: CHS has never been in compliance with court orders from April 2014, September 2014, and April 2021, which all required full staffing of all discharge planning positions.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Why do you feel that's the case?

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: It is an incredible calling and to work and serve folks who are

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: in custody can be quite a daunting professional challenge.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: There's also some practical considerations.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: It's a tough commute.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: And so it can be difficult to find folks who have that level of skill and who are also called to do this work.

utterances.speaker: Ellie Epstein
utterances.text: And it's a real testament to the incredible team that we have, that we have the kind of retention rate, and that we have been able to recruit as many talented, wonderful professionals as we have.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers turns to her bill, Intro 809, and asks how many lock-ins occurred in 2026, their reasons, average duration, and how many lasted over four hours. Boyd and Caputo say they do not have that data and will follow up, prompting the chair to criticize DOC for opposing the bill without lock-in data.
chapters.title: Chair questions lock-in data and Intro 809 rationale

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Pivoting to my bill, Intro 809.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many lock-ins have occurred across the department facilities in 2026?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I don't have that raw data unique to appointments or just in general.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just in general.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Yeah, I would have to follow up with you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm always asking the questions.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can someone check in so you can get it to us?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We can try.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What do you find is the most reasons for lock-ins?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I would turn it over to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: I don't have specific data, but reasons that encompass a lock-in could be for a tactical search operation, obviously an emergency in reference to an incident.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: Those are the most prevalent reasons for a lockdown of a unit.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What is the average duration of a lock-in?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: I don't have specific data in reference to how long is the average, but we do try to lift the lockdown as soon as it's safe to do so.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: So we are very limited in that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many lock-ins have lasted more than four hours?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: Again, I can follow up with that information.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So the concern I'm about to have now, because my bill is about lock-ins, I would imagine that you all would come with data about the lock-ins.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do you have any data available today for us to talk about the lock-ins?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: We did not supply data in reference to lock-in specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So how, in this oversight hearing, is the department going to help to inform us in terms of

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: this legislation and whether or not it's something that is feasible or not because the department came with an opinion about the bill, but yet no data.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm not following that.

chapters.summary: Boyd says DOC data show 0.1% of scheduled medical appointments were rescheduled due to lock-ins from January through August 2026. He defends safety-driven lockdowns and says DOC tries to produce people the same day when possible.
chapters.title: Boyd cites 0.1% missed medical appointments and clinic dashboard

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: So the one data set we do have is specific to medical appointments that are scheduled.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And in regards to appointments that were, you know, rescheduled due to lock-in, that was 0.1%.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so the department has made a lot of progress when it comes to producing individuals in custody to their appointment.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Especially during a lockdown, when it's safe to do so.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And Councilmember, you've been in our facilities and you've seen the corridors.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: If something's happening on one side, an incident that's happening on one side of the building, we're not going to move people around until it's safe to do so, especially with a population who might either retaliate or react to another person in custody in the corridors.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We want to be very conscientious of that.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: But we work very closely with CHS that if someone has missed their medical appointment due to a lock-in, we try to see if they can be produced the same day.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so that's progress.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: In addition, again, this clinic production dashboard, I think, is the path forward to strengthen that coordination, track things in real time.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I welcome the opportunity for you to come.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Tour GRVC and see the clinic production dashboard yourself and engage with uniformed staff to see how it's working.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: We think, you know, modernization is the key here.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: You know, we can follow up when it comes to specific lockdown incidents, but it's all incident driven, right?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Each situation is unique.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so I would just take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Lockdowns are not just a broad brush, right?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: It's incident driven.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: depending on whatever the situation is that precipitated it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The 0.1% that you mentioned, is that for 2026?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: January 2026 through August 2026.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how DOC notifies CHS when a lock-in begins and how CHS prioritizes missed appointments. Boyd describes daily facility-level communication and huddles, while Merrill and Otonichar say CHS is not notified in advance of emergency lock-ins but triages based on acuity, medication adherence, and stability.
chapters.title: Chair asks how DOC notifies CHS during lock-ins and prioritizes care

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And how does DOC notify CHS when a lock-in begins?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I mean, that's constant conversations, right?

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: The wardens are very much aware, and you can speak to the abbreviation of the HSA from CHS that are assigned to the jail.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: Each facility has an HSA assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: The warden and their leadership team are having various daily conversations with the HSAs.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there's additional titles or leadership.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: CHS could speak better to that, but these are ongoing conversations that they facilitate these engagement efforts to see what's going on with specific individual custodians, how we can produce people, if there are challenges to produce people.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so that's ongoing.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: It's happening right now.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: It happens every day.

utterances.speaker: James Boyd
utterances.text: And so it's, yes, that's the best way I can, I guess, answer your question.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So for CHS, are you generally notified before the lock-in begins?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do you know at what part you're notified?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: We wouldn't be notified in advance if it were an emergency lock-in.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: We, of course, would know if someone wasn't produced to an appointment, at which point we would work to reschedule the individual based on acuity.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And are the lock-ins only when, like, a crisis moment happens, to your point?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is that the only time the lock-ins are happening?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: So if we have credible information that needs to be investigated, that can be a reason, obviously, that we would lock down a unit for investigation into action.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: No intelligence or.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And in that moment, are you notifying CHS in advance?

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: So it's not going to be in advance unless it's something that is pre-scheduled.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: Most of those, obviously, events are not pre-scheduled events unless it's a search, which, again, we would notify them as close to the event as possible just to make sure that we are able to conduct a thorough search in a–

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: Surprise nature.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: We have daily huddles with CHS.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: We are in constant communication with them.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: We have officers that are assigned to the clinic that work in conjunction with CHS.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: So the officers in the clinic will be immediately notified, and then our partners would also be notified.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: Just because an area is locked down doesn't mean that we cannot produce that person, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: And it's escalated based on the nature of the appointment and the emergent need for that person to be produced.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Caputo
utterances.text: If an individual is needed, they will be produced.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How does CHS prioritize patients for appointments missed because of a lock-in?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So I'm not even specific to lock-ins, but any time there is a missed appointment, we're looking at clinical acuity need.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: We look at medication adherence, any incidents documented, what were they looking like in their most recent visit, what has been their level of stability.

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Those sorts of factors are taken into account as to...

utterances.speaker: Joseph Otonichar
utterances.text: Prioritization and triaging.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What information does CHS need from the department to safely manage care during a lock-in?

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: So I think because a lock-in is just this temporary moment in time, I wouldn't necessarily focus non-production to clinic on lock-in.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: I think it's broader.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: I think the work, as referenced earlier, that our health services administrators are doing with the officers in the clinic and conversations that are happening at the leadership level are really to address the systemic

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: production challenges.

utterances.speaker: Jeanette Merrill
utterances.text: For our purposes, whether someone missed an appointment because of court or lock-in or barbershop or any number of reasons, it wouldn't change our clinical assessment and need for continued care.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Arden Armbruster introduces herself and Claire Salant from the Independent Budget Office. She says IBO is monitoring the jail population in light of Rikers closure and will share preliminary analysis on people in DOC custody with mental illness and or homelessness.
chapters.title: IBO's Arden Armbruster introduces analysis of mental illness and homelessness in jail population

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Brooks Powers and members of the Committee on Criminal Justice.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: My name is Arden Armbruster, and I'm a lead budget and policy analyst at the New York City Independent Budget Office, IBO.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: I'm joined today by my colleague, Claire Saland.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO is a government agency whose mission is to enhance understanding of New York City's budget, public policy, and economy through independent analysis.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: We appreciate the invitation to testify today at today's hearing on mental health care in New York City's jails.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO has been closely monitoring the changing jail population in light of the mandate to close the facilities on Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Today, we will share preliminary analysis from a forthcoming publication about people in DOC custody with a history of mental illness and or homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: While previous IBO publications have noted that the city has diverted many people facing lower-level charges, the jail population is still larger than the capacity of the borough-based jails.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: The rates of mental illness among people in custody have historically been higher than the general public, but the share of the jail population with mental health needs has been increasing even as the city has expanded its diversion programs.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: However, the overall population with a mental illness is not homogenous.

chapters.summary: Armbruster says IBO analyzed DOC jail stay data through June 2026 and identified two groups: people with co-occurring mental illness and homelessness and people with mental illness alone. She notes data limitations, including lack of markers for serious mental illness, substance use disorder, and domestic violence.
chapters.title: IBO identifies two populations and data limitations

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: To understand this population in more detail, IBO analyzed DOC jail stay data through the end of June 2026.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: identified two distinct populations with mental health needs in DOC custody, those with co-occurring histories of homelessness and those with a history of mental illness alone.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Though this hearing is focused on mental health, we cannot talk about this population without also talking about housing needs.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Of the 19,000 unique people discharged in fiscal year 2026,

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: 58% had a history of mental illness, 30% had a history of mental illness and homelessness, and 26% had a history of mental illness, a history of homelessness, and a prior stay in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Because DOC stay data was IBO's primary source, our analysis may not include individuals who have histories of mental illness and or homelessness documented in other data, nor does our analysis include other co-occurring needs such as substance use disorder and experience with domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO recognizes the importance of these factors in addressing the needs of people with mental illness, but due to data limitations, we will not be speaking to them in this testimony.

chapters.summary: Armbruster says TGNC and non-binary people are a small share of the jail population but 93% had a history of mental illness and 67% also had homelessness. Cisgender women also had higher rates than cisgender men, and people with homelessness histories tended to be older.
chapters.title: IBO finds higher mental illness and homelessness among TGNC people and cis women

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: IBO found that certain groups of people in custody were more likely to have a history of mental illness and or homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: When looking at differences across gender, IBO found that while transgender, gender nonconforming, and non-binary people, TGNC and BI people,

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: are a very small share of the jail population, they have higher rates of mental illness and homelessness than cisgender people in custody.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: 93% had a history of mental illness, and 67% also had a co-occurring history of homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: They were also more likely to have a prior stay.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Cisgender women, who make up about 10% of the jail population in 2026, were also more likely to have a history of mental illness and a co-occurring history of homelessness compared with cisgender men.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Given the higher level of mental health and housing support needed among TGNC and BI people and cisgender women, increasing services for complex needs would support these groups in particular.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: People with a history of homelessness also tend to be older, including people with a co-occurring history of mental illness and particularly people who also have a prior jail stay.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Among those with a prior stay, the median age for people with neither a history of homelessness nor mental illness was 33.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: For people who had history of both, the median age was 39.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: The link between incarceration, accelerated aging, and poor health outcomes has been well established.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Outside of carceral settings, people are typically considered older adults beginning at age 65.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: In correctional settings, that threshold is 55.

chapters.summary: Armbruster says people with both mental illness and homelessness histories typically faced less severe charges, with petty larceny most common, while those with mental illness alone had assault charges at rates similar to people with neither history. She reports longer lengths of stay for the same charges and lower bail payment rates.
chapters.title: IBO reports charges, length of stay, and bail outcomes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We'll now talk about charges and length of stay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: The remainder of this testimony focuses on people with a prior stay only, so people who've returned to custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: People with a history of mental illness and a co-occurring history of homelessness typically face less severe charges than those with solely a history of mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: In recent years, people with a history of both needs were half as likely to be charged with the most serious charge, an A or B felony, as people with a history of neither need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: The most common charge for those with a history of both needs discharged in fiscal year 2026 was petty larceny.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: In contrast, people with a history of mental illness alone, without a history of homelessness, were charged with A or B felonies at similar rates to those with a history of neither need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Their most common charge in fiscal year 26 was assault in the second degree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: People with documented histories of mental health needs also have longer lengths of stay for the same charges than people without a history of mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: For example, the median length of stay on a second-degree assault charge for people discharged in fiscal year 26 was six days for individuals with neither history,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: 36 days for individuals with a history of mental illness alone, and 74 days for individuals with a history of both mental illness and homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Lastly, in fiscal year 26, people with a history of mental illness had bail set at similar rates to other populations, but paid bail at a lower rate, especially those with a co-occurring history of homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: People with both needs paid bail in just 9% of their stays where bail was set, compared with 39%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: among people with neither a history of mental illness nor homelessness were bare well set.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: In summary, as the city considers how to support people with mental health needs who come into contact with the criminal legal system, IBO's findings show that these populations have distinct characteristics and therefore needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Further details will be shared in our forthcoming report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to testify, and we look forward to answering your questions.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how IBO performed the analysis. Armbruster says IBO uses charter-mandated DOC data from fiscal years 2008 through 2026, identifies Brad H. class members and competency restoration discharges, and matches address data to shelter and homeless keywords.
chapters.title: Chair asks IBO how it conducted the analysis

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you explain how you did your analysis?

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So IBO has, through our charter mandated powers to receive data from city agencies,

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: has data on every state in DOC custody from fiscal year 2008 through 2026.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: We use that data to identify people who were sort of ever in the data set, either flagged for a Brad H.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Class member, so someone who is likely receiving mental health care in city jails,

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: and or had a discharge to state hospital for competency restoration.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So that's how we identified people with a mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And our numbers may differ from some other reported numbers because we are looking across multiple stays, given that many people do have very short stays in custody.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: It's not uncommon to see stays of five days.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: days or fewer.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And so people may not make it through all of the processes to be identified as someone with a mental illness in those short stays.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: As it relates to people with a history of homelessness, we did a couple of different things.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: We used the address data in the DOC data that we have available to identify keywords.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So sometimes you'll just see in that address data homeless or shelter.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So we flagged those keywords as well as matched to shelter addresses that IBO also is aware of.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And again, we looked across people's histories to identify people in case they weren't flagged when they had those very short stays.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks IBO to expand on data constraints. Armbruster says IBO cannot identify serious mental illness specifically in its data, nor substance use disorder or domestic violence histories, though those factors matter for programs and diversion.
chapters.title: Chair asks IBO about data constraints

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You mentioned data constraints.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you expand on that?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What data do you need?

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So I think in particular with this analysis, what we wanted to make clear is that this intersection of mental health needs and housing needs is not the only intersection that people should be aware of.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So something, for example, we don't look specifically at serious mental illness because in the data that we have available, we don't have a marker for that specifically.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So data limitations like that, similarly substance use disorder or a history of experience with domestic violence, those other factors that are often considered when

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: creating programs and diversion programs for these populations.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks if IBO has recommendations and how much the city spends on mental health care in custody. Armbruster says IBO does not make recommendations but hopes its report informs policymakers, and says she can follow up on spending and how it is split between DOC and CHS.
chapters.title: Chair asks IBO about recommendations and mental health spending

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are there specific recommendations to address the mental health crisis in jails?

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: So IBO doesn't make recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: However, we do hope that our forthcoming report and this testimony can help policymakers

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: develop programs, as you so decide, that are responsive to the complex needs of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: And so we hope that our forthcoming report will dive a little bit deeper into that to support your decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And do you know how much the city spends on mental health care for people that are in custody with the department?

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: I did not bring that with us today, but that is something that we can certainly look into and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And when you let us know, it'll be good to know also how is that spending separated between DOC and CHS?

utterances.speaker: Arden Armbruster
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you for your testimony.

utterances.text: I now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts for such recordings to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's hearing topic, mental health care in New York City jails.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Please provide a copy of that testimony to the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: For in-person panelists, please come up to the table once your name has been called.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And now I will call the first panel and I will just say, I ask that everyone please adhere to the two minute limit.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You can submit additional testimony in writing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So just so that we have a smooth public testimony process, I ask again that everyone adhere to the two minute limit.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Limit because we do have a number of people signed up and we want to hear from everyone.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So for the first panel, we are going to have Barbara Hamilton.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And Raji.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: From the New York County Defender Services.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You can begin when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
