chapters.summary: Barbara Hamilton of the Legal Aid Society says her office sees people in acute mental health crisis being met with isolation and punitive measures. She describes clients allegedly deadlocked for long periods on Rikers, including in the PACE unit, and urges oversight of DOC and CHS.
chapters.title: Barbara Hamilton testifies on deadlocking and punitive care for mentally ill clients

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and Committee Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: My name is Barbara Hamilton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: I am the Director of the Incarcerated Client Services Unit at the Legal Aid Society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: I'm going to comment on mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: Every day, my office sees people who are in acute crisis over mental health issues at the Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: We talk to people in the city jails who have serious mental illness or in psychosis, thinking of self-harm and just trying to receive care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: And often what we see is that they are met with isolation and punitive measures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: So, for example, we have a client who has been deadlocked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: For about a year on and off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: Our staff reported this individual was having hallucinations, and there was no meaningful treatment until there was an act of self-harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: We have another client who was deadlocked in the PACE unit, who had suffered from serious mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: She was not receiving recreation, access to programming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: When staff went to see her, her clothes were visibly stained with menstrual blood, and she was using cereal boxes to make sanitary products.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: We have this matter in court, and we're now in contempt proceedings because the Department of Correction is not obeying a court order to allow this client out of cell time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: So generally what we see is a punitive system that is failing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: has an important role to play, and we urge them to exercise this oversight of DOC and CHS, demand transparency

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: about what's happening in these units, scrutinize and end the use of isolation and restrictive practices,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: as well as supporting housing, alternate programs for incarceration and treatment so people don't end up in jail in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks Hamilton to confirm that her clients were allegedly deadlocked by DOC and when those instances occurred. Hamilton says the cases are from 2026 and that Legal Aid is in contempt proceedings over two court orders. Brooks-Powers asks her to provide documentation to committee staff.
chapters.title: Chair follows up with Hamilton on 2026 deadlocking court orders

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And just a follow-up question to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So just to confirm, you're saying that you have several clients that have been allegedly deadlocked.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: At Department of, like within the Department of Corrections?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: Yes, and there's actually two core orders in place, and we're in contempt proceedings in two cases because the Department of Correction has not filed those core orders to clients who have been deadlocked.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And when were these instances that they took place?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Were they in 2026 or prior to?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: One client we had that didn't have a court order was 2025 to 2026, but we have two individuals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: The cases are live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: They're happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: So we're talking off the top of my head, winter, spring of 2026 and continuing to this day.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: If you would not mind to provide the committee staff information about those instances so we can follow up with the department because they just testified under oath that there has not been any deadlocking.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I'd like to follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Barbara Hamilton
utterances.text: Yes, we can provide the copy of the court orders and any pleadings that we've initiated to this committee.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Raji Deyat Mangalam, a clinical social worker with New York County Defender Services, shares success stories of clients diverted to community treatment. He argues community recovery is possible and asks the council to support the Treatment Court Expansion Act on its Albany agenda.
chapters.title: Raji Deyat Mangalam urges community treatment and Treatment Court Expansion Act

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and Committee Member, and thank you so much for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: My name is Raji Deyat Mangalam, and I'm a licensed clinical social worker and senior policy social worker at New York County Defender Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: I'm here to testify that community recovery and reintegration are not a pie in the sky.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: I want to share about two clients who might have been written off as lost causes, but for many of us banding together and refusing to give up on community-based solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: When I first met my client, I'll call Harry, to protect his confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: He'd been street homeless for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: He was severely depressed, had serious opioid use issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: He was estranged from his family and facing a long prison sentence on numerous violent felony charges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: By every measure the systems use, there was no hope for Harry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: After great many struggles on Harry's part and a great deal of advocacy to get in the right community services, he turned the corner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: He began to excel in every aspect of his ATI mandate, and he graduated from Manhattan's Felony ATI Court with flying colors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: A few years have passed, and Harry continues to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: He's well, he's a working taxpayer, he's reconnected with his family, and he remains stably integrated in the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: One employer even wrote to the ATI court, I truly mean it that I'd hire 15 Harrys if I could.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: Another NYCDS client, whom I'll call Tom, was extremely

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: extremely ill when his attorney met him at arraignment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: And he was charged with a violent felony, homeless, completely disorganized in thought and speech, and had been in the throes of untreated schizophrenia for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: He also struggled in various ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: He also had substance use issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: And what I'm going to say is that the DA objected to treatment court, but the judge saw something in Tom and gave him his real first chance at community integration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: In respect for the time, I'm going to cut short and say that at his ATI graduation, the DA said, quote, you have proven us wrong, quote, and called watching his journey inspiring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: Neither Harry nor Tom recovered at Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: They recovered because many of us fought to get them into services in the community, and because in Tom's case, a judge was willing to overrule a prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: Let's just take a step back for a moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: We've tried caging human beings in estate-run asylums.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: We then shifted to a whack-a-mole approach since 1963, and now that's what got us to where we are today with yesterday's asylum and today's Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: In the morning, we were talking about outposted therapeutic housing units in our latest iteration of what I fear is whack-a-mole.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to wrap up, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: And I would say that the time to invest in community infrastructure is now, and that I would say that treatment courts provide critical case management and oversight, holding both participants and community programs accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: We at, in finishing, we at New York County Defender Services are asking the council to support and put the Treatment Court Expansion Act on your Albany agenda without any further delay so that we can divert as many people as possible away from jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raji Deyat Mangalam
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You can submit the rest in writing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next panel, Ethan Lowe with Legal Aid, Camilla Ruda, Legal Aid Society,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Rachel Golden, Maya Zellkind, Lucas Marquez.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Ask everybody to please adhere to the two-minute limit.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And you can begin once you're ready.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just come off of mute.

chapters.summary: Ethan Lowe of the Legal Aid Society and the TGNC-NBI task force says conditions remain urgent for trans and gender nonconforming people in DOC custody. He supports Intro 133 with advocate amendments and urges a hearing on Intro 134 for enforceable gender-aligned housing protections.
chapters.title: Ethan Lowe testifies on TGNC task force and gender-aligned housing denials

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: My name is Ethan Lowe, and I am a staff attorney in the LGBTQ Law and Policy Unit at the Legal Aid Society and a member of the New York City Task Force on Issues Faced by TGNC and BI People.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: That is transgender, gender nonconforming, nonbinary, and intersex people in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: The task force was created in 2019 following the death of Lailene Polanco, a transgender woman who died on Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: Her death brought attention to the dangerous conditions that TGNC and BI New Yorkers have long reported experiencing in DOC custody, including unsafe housing placements and high rates of violence and harassment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: The task force was established to examine these conditions and recommend changes to DOC policies and practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: Those conditions remain urgent today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: TG and CNBI people, particularly transgender women and trans feminine people, continue to be involuntarily placed in men's facilities where they face heightened risk of physical and sexual violence and the daily psychological harm of being confined in a setting that denies their identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: Those seeking safer gender-aligned housing must navigate an opaque request process, and DOC's own Fiscal 26 data show that approximately half of gender-aligned housing transfer requests are denied.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: Each denial can leave a person in a facility where they face harassment, violence, isolation, or pressure to conceal their identity simply to survive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: That is why the task force work remains necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: It creates a forum where directly impacted people, advocates, and government agencies can identify systemic failures and press for solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: We support Intro 133 to extend the task force because the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: City must continue that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: The renewal must come with structural changes needed for the task force to function effectively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: We urge the council to adopt the amendments proposed by the advocates of the task force and pass Intro 133 as amended.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: We also urge that the city hears Intro 134, which is a bill to establish enforceable protections around gender-aligned housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: Intro 133 extends an important oversight body, but the task force recommendation can only go so far if they're not adopted by DOC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: Intro 134 would directly change policy affecting TGNC and BI people in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ethan Lowe
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Maya Zellkind, a legal intern at Brooklyn Defender Services, reads an account from a formerly incarcerated trans woman. The account describes sexual assault, violence, denial of transfer to a women's facility, and lack of medical care at Rikers.
chapters.title: Maya Zellkind reads testimony from a formerly incarcerated trans woman

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: My name is Maya Zellkind, and I'm a legal intern with the Civil Rights and Law Reform Unit at Brooklyn Defender Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: I want to use my time to bring the voices of TGNC and BI people directly affected by DOC's practices into this hearing to show that the conditions that the task force was established to address continue to exist and our work is not done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: The following is an account of someone formerly placed in Rikers who experienced violence and struggled to navigate a men's facility while targeted for her identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: When I was on Rikers Island, I went through so much because of my gender identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: I experienced being sexually assaulted by officers and inmates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: I'm a transgender female.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: As a transgender female, I wasn't accepted in population with other inmates because they didn't accept anyone in the LGBTQ community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: Corrections officers used to get a kick out of me and other transgender females getting either sexually assaulted or beat up and jumped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: We had no type of protection whatsoever, so me being from the projects in the streets, I had to start to conduct myself in survival mode.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: Before that, I requested for a female facility and was denied numerous times because I didn't have long hair, breasts, butt fat, and I wasn't doing sexual favors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: Gang members all messed around on the low, and they provided some type of protection and security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: So I ended up being around them, but then I ended up being labeled as a gang member because of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: So I started using that as an advantage and ended up putting myself deeper into trouble and not realizing that a lot of transgender people get threatened for their safety and get offered drugs for sex or sexual favors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: I don't do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: I had to figure out a way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: How am I going to protect myself without getting into fights or trouble?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: We get no medical care or medical attention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Camila, a paralegal at the Legal Aid Society and task force member, reads testimony from a formerly incarcerated trans woman. The testimony describes repeated sexual assault, harassment, threats by officers, and the suicide of another trans woman, and urges passage of Intro 133 and hearing Intro 134.
chapters.title: Camila reads testimony on abuse of a trans woman at Rikers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Camila.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I'm a paralegal from the Legal Aid Society who works directly with TGNC incarcerated individuals and I'm also a part of the task force.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I'm here to share testimony from a trans woman who was formerly held in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I made a mistake in my life which landed me incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: At no time did the judge tell me that I would be treated differently, that I would suffer the abuse and torture sustained for merely being myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: A trans woman housed with males sticking out like a blinking red light.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: The abuse, the torture that I sustained was at the hands of the incarcerated males and the officers alike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: My body was brutally raped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I was sexually assaulted multiple times, groped many times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I was horrifically threatened, escorted, extorted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I had on with urine thrown on me and semen thrown into my face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: Called derogatory names daily.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: All of this was the norm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I asked the officer for help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: He told me that you're housed with males.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: Deal with it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: They will find you hanging here and they will rule it as suicide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: The trans woman

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: in the cell next to mine, she couldn't take the abuse any longer, and she took her life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: Intro 134 would have saved me from all this abuse and the torture that my body was placed through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I am a person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I am a human being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: We are all collectively constituents here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: We have families, friends, and loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: We deserve safety, respect, and dignity, just the same as any other human being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: I am forever altered by the trauma that I was forced to endure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: We urge the council to extend the task force by passing Intro 133.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: And I will add that we can also please add intro 134 to the agenda, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Camila
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Cabán states for the record that she is a co-sponsor of Intro 134 and requested it be part of the hearing. She says she hopes the committee will hear the bill at some point.
chapters.title: Cabán confirms co-sponsorship and requests hearing on Intro 134

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And just for the record, I am a co-sponsor on Intro 134 and requested that it be a part of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I am hopeful that we are able to hear that bill at some point.

chapters.summary: Lucas Marquez of Brooklyn Defender Services and the task force supports Intro 133 but says amendments are needed. He describes structural problems including lack of administrative support, uneven agency participation, and DOC opacity, and proposes Board of Correction administration, qualified representatives, reporting, and consultation requirements.
chapters.title: Lucas Marquez proposes task force amendments to Intro 133

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: My name is Lucas Marquez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: I'm the Director of Law Reform at Brooklyn Defender Services, and I work with our jail services team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: I've served on the task force since 2023.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: The task force advocates want to support Intro 133, but believe amendments are needed, and I'll just explain why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: At the outset, I want to emphasize that we are eager to work with DOC and CHS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: We understand that it's vital in doing so to reduce the risk, violence, and indignity that people face when they're placed in a DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: But over the last several years, the task force produced important work despite serious structural problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: It has lacked dedicated administrative support, the ability to obtain information, and to move its work forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: Agency participation has been uneven.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: Representatives frequently did not have the relevant experience, authority to answer critical questions, or buy-in to push changes in the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: DOC has not been transparent in providing key policies or providing important updates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: For years, and as you heard today, we were told that the principal directive governing the treatment and housing of trans, intersex, and gender non-binary people was under revision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: But at no point were we given details about that process or advised or engaged to opine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: The result is that there had been no changes to that directive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: Furthermore, major decisions were made about department actions that seriously impact

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: trans and non-binary population without informing us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: For example, people housed at RMSC where the special consideration unit is located were transferred to an entirely different correctional system as part of the emergency response at Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: Another example is that people housed in RMSC units and PC were merged in order to allow cis men into RMSC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: However, in neither of these instances was a task force consulted or even provided details about these actions after implementation, even though these moves created obvious risks for trans non-binary people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: Our amendments respond directly to these failures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: They give the Board of Correction responsibility for administering the task force.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: They require agencies to designate representatives with relevant experience and sufficient authority to participate meaningfully.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: The amendments require facility tools and meaningful opportunities to hear from people in custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: They require agencies to provide relevant policies and written notice of changes, improve reporting, and require consultation with the task force.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to wrap up, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: In consultation with the task force before major changes impacting people are implemented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lucas Marquez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Rachel Golden, a psychologist and task force member, says the 2022 task force report made detailed recommendations on intake, housing, mental health, reentry, staffing, and accountability. She says virtually none have been implemented and urges Intro 133 with amendments and a prompt hearing on Intro 134.
chapters.title: Rachel Golden says task force recommendations remain unimplemented and urges Intro 134

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: My name is Rachel Golden, and I am a member of the task force and have been since 2022.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: I'm a psychologist and forensic evaluator and have worked extensively with people in custody in our city jails and state prisons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: In August of 2022, the task force published a comprehensive report on the treatment and housing of TGNC and NBI people in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: The report did not just identify problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: It offered detailed recommendations on intake, housing, mental health and wellness, reentry, staffing and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: Those recommendations were grounded in the experiences of TGNC NBI people in custody and in years of work by directly impacted members, advocates, and agency representatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: Four years later, virtually none of these recommendations have been implemented, and we are not aware of corresponding changes to DOC's housing policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: TGNC and BI people are still routed through gender misaligned intake, denied safer housing, and left without a meaningful and transparent way to challenge those decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: The fiscal year 26 denial figures show that the problem is continuing, not resolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: This is why the council should have heard 134 today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: 133 renews the task force and advisory body.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: 134 addresses the underlying policies that this advisory body has spent years asking the city to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: 134 would actually establish enforceable protections around gender-aligned housing, clearer procedures, and review when a request is denied, and greater transparency and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: accountability in DOC's decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: The non-governmental advocates of the task force have identified Intro 134 as our number one legislative priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: Renewing the task force while declining even to hold a hearing on its central recommendations risks asking impacted people and advocates to repeat the same work without an actual path to implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: The task force can document and recommend as we had since our inception, but it cannot compel DOC to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: If the council is serious about addressing the conditions TGNC and VI people face inside, it should pass Intro 133 with the Advocates'amendments, and it should promptly hold a public hearing on Intro 134.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: The city should not treat continuing the task force as a substitute for action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rachel Golden
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you to this panel.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We'll next have Zachary Katson-Nelson with Independent Rikers Commission, Victor Herrera from Freedom Agenda, and Darren Mack with Freedom Agenda.

chapters.summary: Darren Mack, co-director of Freedom Agenda and a Rikers survivor, says many members struggle to get mental health services and face crisis before jail. He cites rising serious mental illness and recidivism, and asks for budget investments in low-barrier housing, dual diagnosis treatment, competency restoration, and community mental health teams.
chapters.title: Darren Mack calls for diversion, housing, and budget investments

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Brooks-Powers and committee members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: Thank you for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: My name is Darren Mack, and I'm a co-director of Freedom Agenda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: I'm a survivor of Rikers, and our members are people who have experienced Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: We also coordinate the campaign to close Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: Many of our members have struggled to get mental health services at Rikers or tried to help their family members get services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: They've also experienced the tragic irony of waiting months or years for quality treatment in the community and then finding a jail cell offered immediately once they reach the point of crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: The experiences are reflected in the data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: There are over 1,500 people at Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: Ireland who are diagnosed with a serious mental illness and that number has increased by 83% since 2022.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: 49.6% of people leaving Rikers with a mental health diagnosis return within a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: These numbers are shameful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: There is no one solution to address this, but there are many actions the mayor and city council can take immediately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: By diverting as many people as possible, as quickly as possible, DOC and CHS stand a much better chance of improving care for a smaller number of people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: For example, they could house everyone with serious mental illness, mental health needs, and dedicated units with clinical staff on a unit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: We need investments in community-based programs that cannot wait another nine months or more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: City Hall should make substantial investments in the November budget modification to start addressing this crisis, including

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: at least $20.3 million to immediately open 150 units of low-barrier housing for people with court involvement and mental health diagnosis, a $3 million capital investment to open more dual diagnosis residential treatment capacity,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: At least $1.7 million to develop an outpatient competency restoration pilot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: Sufficient funding to open the remaining 132 GISH units previously promised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: Sufficient funding to eliminate the wait list for community-based mental health treatment teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: And other recommendations outlined in our full written testimony and our countdown to closing the Rikers policy brief.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: In conclusion, we look forward to continue to work with the city council to ensure that everyone's DOC custody can get the health care they need and get support and community ensure they don't return.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: And I echo the advocate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: recommendations that the council and the committee endorse and pass intro 134.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Darren Mack
utterances.text: Thank you for letting me testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Victor Herrera, a formerly directly impacted Rikers survivor, says behavioral health emergencies need clinical responses and community-based support. He supports closing Rikers and the Treatment Court Expansion Act and criticizes CHS and DOC approaches to mental health crises.
chapters.title: Victor Herrera urges clinicians in crisis response and closing Rikers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair, members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak today about the urgent intersection of mental health, public safety, and conditions at Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: My name is Victor Herrera, a formerly directly impacted Rikers survivor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: I appreciate the Council's attention to the policies that connect people experiencing behavioral health crisis with appropriate care, protect the safety,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: and dignity of those in custody and reduce the use of incarceration where treatment and community-based support would better serve both individuals and the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: It is more the reason that I stand for community-based support aligned with those with the closed Rikers and Treatment Court Expansion Act, both of which would fast-track reduction of the jail population and finally putting Rikers Island in our past and moving forward with truth in public health and treatment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Behavioral health emergencies require response that protects immediate safety while addressing the clinical conditions driving the crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Integrating licensed mental health clinicians into public safety systems gives responders access to clinical assessments, trauma-informed de-escalation, and direct pathways to care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Improve access to care intervention at critical phases of such encounters of people experiencing mental health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Clinicians can arrange referrals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: safety planning, follow-up, and connection to community-based services rather than relying solely on transport, citation, or arrest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Linking individuals to ongoing treatment and social support can address underlying needs that otherwise generate repeated emergency calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: These links and referrals should expand the greater need for intense mobile treatment if a triage of public health remedies is allocated locally at each of the city's central booking stations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Unlike correctional health services post-treatment on Rikers Island, testimony for you today, I would have to ask this committee to look at the crisis compared to responses by CHS health clinicians and how such approaches have not met the need for people experiencing mental health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Words such as DOC, overriding security, management, and disciplinary and involuntary hospitalization has been a serious underlying factor of people losing their lives to mental health and treatment solely because CHS will offer before you to justify

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: NYCDOC continued detention of people with mental health concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: I have shared my own testimony and full proposals toward a more robust approach to treating people with mental health and chemical dependency concerns during response to arrest and prior to detention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victor Herrera
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Zachary Katznelson of the Independent Rikers Commission says DOC's response to deadlocking appears to have been only telling staff to stop, with no new training or inspections. He also criticizes fragmented discharge and housing coordination, saying no agency is overseeing whether people get connected to care.
chapters.title: Zachary Katznelson criticizes deadlocking response and reentry coordination

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: I'm Zachary Ketz-Nelson with the Independent Rikers Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: Thanks for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: I want to echo the budget concerns that Darren raised and support those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: And just talk about a couple things that came up in the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: Deadlocking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: Disappointed to hear from the Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: It sounded like the only thing they changed when deadlocking came to light was to tell people to stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: It's the same type of supervision they had before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: There's no new training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: There's no new inspections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: Nothing has changed except don't do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: And what has happened over the last several years is that training that staff did receive, crisis intervention training, which was a national model where correction staff and health care staff trained together, then worked as teams in those units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: That has completely fallen apart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: It fell apart during COVID.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: It has been brought back in a watered-down, halfway form.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: Correction Department and CHS don't train together anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: They train completely separately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: And we see the results.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: As you alluded, staff feel like they don't have a choice but to resort because they don't know what else to do but deadlock people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: And that is utterly wrong to them and particularly to the people that are being deadlocked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: That has to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: In terms of people getting out, I just want to mention a couple things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: One is that, as you know well, over 1,000 people a year get approved for supportive housing at Rikers, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: Almost all of them end up in the streets or in the shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: There are systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: We have emergency transitional housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: People could be in there if they're not getting directly into supportive housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: But it's falling apart, and it's falling apart in large part because there is no city agency that's active.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: actually in charge of making sure that people get what they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: As in, CHS does its part, then they hand it off to DOHMH, and HRA is involved, and DSS, and all these different entities, but nobody is overarching, nobody is looking over this whole thing and saying, is this actually working, are we getting people connected with the care?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: Providers don't know that people are getting out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: They're not told they're being released.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: They don't meet people before they come out, which is a huge factor in success, people actually using the services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: There are lots of things we know we could do, and I really hope that when the administration releases its plan to close Rikers, that they're going to address these types of real bureaucratic failures that are preventing people from getting care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Zachary Katznelson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you to the panel.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Giselle Castro with Exalt Youth, Tarini Garamella, Osborne Association, Nadia Chite with Cases,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Miriam Goodman with Women's Prison Association.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm also going to add Jeanette Bacanegra with Justice for Families, LTD.

chapters.summary: Dr. Gisele Castro of Exalt says young people affected by the criminal legal system carry untreated trauma and grief. She supports Intros 133, 453, and 809 but says laws do not deliver care, and recommends multi-year flexible contracts for frontline organizations and a formal community role in implementation.
chapters.title: Gisele Castro calls for flexible community contracts and implementation role

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: Good afternoon and thank you Chair Brooks Powers and the members of the committee for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: My name is Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: Giselle Castro and I am the CEO of Exalt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: I have spent over 20 years working in and around the criminal justice system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: And what I know is this, the young people that Exalt serves are ages 15 through 19.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: And they have never been given a clean slate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: They come to us with trauma, with grief and anxiety that no one has ever named, let alone treated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: I will reference a young person experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: As a teenager, this young New Yorker experienced family violence and became involved with the child welfare system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: They were struggling with grief and with their emotional, psychological well-being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: But the support that they needed was missing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: When they came to Exalt, someone showed up for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: Through consistent mentorship, advocacy, educational guidance, and opportunities, she is now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: and this person is in higher education, completing their graduate degree in future mental health, wanting to participate in changing a system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: This story is not an exception, it's the pattern, and it's what extols supports for the proposal that were and are still being discussed today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: Intro 133 recognizes that representation in form of public policy matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: Intro 453 recognizes that children with incarcerated loved ones carry that weight too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: And intro 809 recognizes that care can't disappear whenever a facility locks down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: But laws don't deliver care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: People do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: What I recommend, what we recommend are two things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: First is the multi-year flexible contracts for frontline organizations so that their work completely does not stop when funding cycle ends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: And lastly, the second one is a formal role for community organization in implementing these bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: And thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gisele Castro
utterances.text: I will submit a copy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Tarini Garamella of the Osborne Association testifies for the Rikers Visiting Workgroup on Intro 453. She says the bill is well-intentioned but too vague and would inappropriately expand DOC into assessing and referring children for mental health services, urging community-based services instead.
chapters.title: Tarini Garamella opposes Intro 453 as vague and DOC-led

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: My name is Terini Garamella, and I'm a policy associate for the Osborne Association.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: I'm testifying on behalf of the community members of the Rikers Visiting Workgroup in regards to Intro 453.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: My testimony outlines ways in which this bill is too vague as written and could lead to harmful practices, and my written testimony will share more in-depth recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: We believe this bill is well-intentioned, and we are eager to collaborate with Chair Stevens to strengthen this legislation to support the mental well-being of children who have incarcerated parents on Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: This bill was originally introduced in 2018, and we and several of our partners opposed it then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: We are deeply concerned about how this bill will expand DOC's role into assessing and providing referrals for children to access mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: We should instead be investing in community-based services and improving the visiting experience for children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: We agree with DOC that they should not be the ones assessing children for referrals and providing mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: DOC currently struggles to provide adequate mental health care and support to the people in their custody and their staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: It seems outside the scope of DOC's mission and expertise and is an unnecessary burden to now add children, many of whom DOC has no background information, history, or understanding of their needs, to the list of those in their care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: Instead, information about community-based mental health resources could be made available at the Central Visit House and on DOC visitor buses so families can voluntarily connect themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: to services they feel would benefit them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: Visiting Rikers is still such a traumatizing and dehumanizing experience for children and families and the incarcerated people they visit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: Under the best of circumstances, it is exhausting, stressful, and includes leaving your loved one behind, worrying about their well-being and safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: The best way to support children and families'physical, mental, and emotional health is to ensure their interactions with DOC staff are child-sensitive and child-friendly and that their visits are protected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: And ultimately, we must collectively work together to expedite the closure of Rikers Island and return their loved ones home safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tarini Garamella
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Miriam Goodman of the Women's Prison Association supports the intent of Intro 453 but says care should be provided by trained mental health professionals in trusted community organizations, not by DOC. She argues the system causing harm should not be the system families must trust for healing.
chapters.title: Miriam Goodman says children's mental health care belongs in community

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and member of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: My name is Miriam Goodman, and I'm the Senior Director of Clinical Care at the Women's Prison Association.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: For more than 180 years, WPA has served women impacted by the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: We provide a continuum of care working with people in the community at Rikers, at Bedford Hills, and as they return home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Our work includes case management, housing reentry support, and trauma-responsive clinical care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: We appreciate the intent behind Intro 453 and its recognition that children impacted by a parent's incarceration may need mental health support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: But we, along with other advocates, strongly believe that care should be provided by trained mental health professionals through trusted community-based organizations, not by the Department of Correction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Incarceration impacts entire families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: When a parent is incarcerated, children experience that separation too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Their lives and relationships are disrupted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: We cannot talk about healing without acknowledging the systems that have contributed to that harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: The system that causes or compounds harm cannot also be the system we ask families to trust with their healing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Trauma-responsive care is built on trust, safety, choice, consistency, and relationships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Those things are incredibly difficult to create when care is tied to the very system that many families experience as a source of trauma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Community-based providers can offer something fundamentally different, care that is independent of the correctional system and relationships that do not end when someone leaves a jail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: We see every day what that kind of care can look like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Our team provides individual and group counseling that recognizes the impact of both interpersonal and systemic trauma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: We meet people as the whole, not as a diagnosis, a charge, or a moment in their life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: And because we work across the continuum, relationships can start in community, continuing through incarceration, and back when someone's home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: That is what we believe we should be investing in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: We urge the council to invest in community-based mental health services and fund organizations at levels that allow us to recruit and retain excellent clinicians and provide families with the quality of care they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Healing should be rooted in community with trusted providers who can be there during incarceration, through reentry, and long after someone comes home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miriam Goodman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maya Zellkind
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Nadia Chait of CASES says DOC and CHS described a world that does not match her clients' experiences. She recounts a client with a known release date who missed a long-acting injectable and faced Medicaid and pharmacy failures, causing a 24-hour delay. CASES opposes Intro 453 as written.
chapters.title: Nadia Chait describes discharge medication failure and opposes Intro 453

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: I'm Nadia Cheat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Director of Policy and Advocacy at Cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: We serve over 12,000 New Yorkers annually with a specialty in serving folks with serious mental illness and criminal legal system involvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: DOC and CHS described a world today that I wish existed for our clients, but it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: And it is frustrating to see those agencies continue to state that they are providing adequate care

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: and producing people for their mental health appointments when their own data, as well as the numerous monitors of the city's various consent decrees that they are continually not in compliance with, show that that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: And so I'd like to share a story of one of our clients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: our clients who recently experienced what happens when DOC and CHS fail at their basic duties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: And I would like to state at the front that this was a client with a known release date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: So this is the easiest scenario for them to succeed, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: And this was an individual coming into our Nathaniel Act Alternative to Incarceration program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: The individual was due for their long-acting injectable on the day of their release.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: They did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: The individual's Medicaid should have been active.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: It was set to inpatient, which means that they can't receive community care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: The individual's prescription was not sent to a pharmacy, so even though...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: That prescription would be covered by the city's medication grant program, which is designed to cover that gap when individuals'Medicaid is not active.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: They had no coverage for that prescription.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: And this was an individual who was on electronic monitoring, and so they were very, very hesitant to leave their residence and go somewhere to seek the injection, like a hospital,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: where they could have been forced to wait many hours and where there could have been potential compliance implications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: We were ultimately able to get the medication called into the pharmacy the following day and pick it up and bring it to that individual's residence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: But that was a 24-hour delay in this individual receiving their needed medication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: And this is for people with the best scenario of wraparound care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: So instead, we should really focus on diverting people before they enter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: interact with the system and in earlier stages, which my written testimony details.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: We also oppose intro 453 as written.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadia Chait
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Jeannette Bocanegra of Justice for Families says Intro 453 is misguided and should be rewritten. She says children visiting incarcerated loved ones are not in DOC custody and should not face additional screening or risk of ACS involvement; she urges community-based support instead.
chapters.title: Jeannette Bocanegra strongly opposes Intro 453 as family surveillance risk

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: Peace and blessings, Chair and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: My name is Jeanette Bocanegra and I'm the executive director of a nationally family-led organization in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: I am also a mother and a long-time advocate for families impacted by the juvenile and adult system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: Justice for Families strongly opposes Intro 453.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: Though the intentions are great,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: This bill is misguided and should not be moved forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: It needs to be rewritten.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: We absolutely support providing children with healing and mental health resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: However, the Department of Correction should not assess or provide mental health services to children simply because they are visiting an incarcerated parent or loved one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: The department continues to demonstrate that they need to be improved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: These children are visitors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: They are not in the Department of Corrections custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: Maintaining a relationship with someone they love should not expose them to additional screening, surveillance, labeling them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: And another system involvement with ACS, another system that outcomes are horrible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: We want to shrink those systems and build the community's capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeannette Bocanegra
utterances.text: Families already are traveling long distance and endure long waits, lockdowns, cancellations, visits, and confusing rules.

chapters.summary: Jennifer Parish of the Urban Justice Center Mental Health Project says the city remains out of compliance with longstanding court-ordered discharge planning requirements. She says monitors found quality discharge planning in only slightly over half of cases and connects this to community service gaps.
chapters.title: Jennifer Parish warns discharge planning noncompliance persists

utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: My name is Jennifer Parrish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: I'm the Director of Criminal Justice Advocacy at the Urban Justice Center Mental Health Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: Thank you for convening this hearing on mental health, and thank you, Council, for asking questions specifically related to discharge planning services, because that's a really important component of connecting people who are inside who are receiving mental health treatment with services on the outside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: One thing we didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: about in this hearing is the non-compliance that still goes on despite the fact that there's been a court

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: ordered settlement in place for more than 20 years the city is still not complying with really important components of that specifically related to the quality of discharge planning services that are provided

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: in the latest monitors report they detail the findings specifically related to services that are for people with serious mental illness like applying for public assistance getting connected with supportive housing and also the quality of those services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: in only about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: slightly over half of the cases that the monitors looked at did people get overall quality discharge planning services and I want to connect this with what

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: Nadia Chait said from cases the reason the person they described a perfect example of what happens when someone doesn't get or the kind of situation a person can wind up in if they don't get mental health if they don't get discharge planning services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: and why was this person ultimately

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: caught was because we had cases there who was connected and tried to fill all of the holes in discharge planning that happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: And that connects really to what Zachary Katz Nelson said, is we can't just look at what's going on inside of the jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: We have to connect it to what's happening in the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: If we don't have enough assertive community treatment teams, if we don't have enough supportive housing, if we don't have providers that can connect with discharge planning, it doesn't matter how much we improve that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
