utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Parish
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Marco Barrios of the Urban Justice Center Mental Health Project and Treatment Not Jail Coalition says a punitive setting cannot be therapeutic. He describes limited treatment modalities at Rikers and says psychiatric medication management often ignores patients' needs and histories.
chapters.title: Marco Barrios says punitive jails cannot be therapeutic

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: Good afternoon and thank you for having me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: My name is Marco Barrios.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: I'm the criminal justice advocate at the Mental Health Project of the Urban Justice Center, where my primary responsibility is monitoring New York City's compliance with the Brad Age Settlement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: I'm also a member of the Treatment Not Jail Coalition, which champions the Treatment Court Expansion Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: Furthermore, I'm a veteran in the United States Armed Forces and served in the Gulf War, and I'm also a survivor of the criminal legal system, where I did 24 years and six months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: But now I visit Rikers Island weekly, and I see up to 20 clients each time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: I'm here to tell you what I see in those jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: One, a punitive setting cannot be a therapeutic space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: The forces used to exercise control often makes the things more out of control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: You cannot run a program that promotes recovery, which requires self-direction, respect, and hope inside a system that demands submission, strips people of their humanity,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: and fills them with despair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: Now, mental health treatment in jails and prisons centered primarily around the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: provision of medication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: Medication should not be the only option.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: There should be different modalities of treatment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: At Riker's, other treatment methods are limited at best and for some, non-existent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: The one-on-ones with clinicians are brief and group therapy is also limited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: The treatment plan should be a growing plan that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: provides for the individual needs of each person in response as they change over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: And even if they receive appropriate psychiatric medication, that is a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: Psychiatric medication management is supposed to be ongoing structured partnership between a patient and prescribing provider to evaluate, adjust, and monitor psychotropic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: Medication for safety and effectiveness, and the consequences are predictable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: The individual's previous experience with medication and understanding of the illness is at times ignored.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: Rather than listening and responding to the needs of each person, psychiatric...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: That was quick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: My action is to support the treatment I call...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I have the written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marco Barrios
utterances.text: There's a lot there.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I know.

chapters.summary: Mateo Guerrero of Make the Road New York says trans and queer immigrants are consistently criminalized, citing Operation Restore Roosevelt. He supports Intros 133 and 134, saying gender-aligned housing is necessary to prevent harassment, violence, and fear of seeking basic services.
chapters.title: Mateo Guerrero supports Intros 133 and 134 for trans immigrants

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: It's okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: Chair Brooks, thank you so much for hosting this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: My name is Mateo Guerrero.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: I am an organizer at Make the Road New York, and I'm here to give public testimony on behalf of Make the Road New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: We serve over 30,000 community members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: across New York City for services from immigration to housing to employment discrimination, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: We also have a particular group that serves trans and queer immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: It's called our Trans Immigrant Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: And one of the things that I want to highlight is that trans and queer immigrants are consistently being criminalized very often and facing the potential of being incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: One of the clear examples that we have seen is Operation Restore Roosevelt, which has been ongoing since October 2024.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: It started with...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: The prior administration, Eric Adams, and it's still ongoing under the Mandani administration, criminalizing and particularly targeting sex workers in Jackson Heights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: One of the populations that engages in sex work, particularly, are transgender women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: And the reason why today we're here to show our strong support for Intro 133 as well for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: Intro 134 is because we believe that trans communities, first of all, should not be incarcerated, but if incarcerated, that they receive the support to be able to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: I'm sorry, to be able to have a dignifying life while incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: When incarcerated trans and queer, trans, gender non-binary, and gender non-conforming people who are housed in a facility that does not align with their gender identity, they are often

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: exposed to harassment, violence, discrimination, and oftentimes it also creates a fear to even request basic services, such as

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: hormone replacement therapy out of fear of the interactions they will have with other folks who are incarcerated as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: Being housed in the wrong facility can also force trans and gender expansive folks to constantly have to explain and defend who they are in an environment where they already have very little control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: This is why Intro 133 and 134 are important steps towards addressing these harms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: Intro 133 will strengthen oversight and accountability for how the Department of Correction treats trans and non-binary people in custody, and Intro 134 will require the Department of Corrections to house people according to their gender identity unless they choose otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: This legislation recognizes that something that should not be controversial, which is that trans and gender diverse people should be treated with dignity and respect, including when they're incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateo Guerrero
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Maxima Rodas of Make the Road New York's Trans Immigrant Project says avoiding incarceration is ideal but trans and gender-diverse people face heightened vulnerability. Rodas says housing decisions should consider gender identity and safety, and urges passage of Intros 133 and 134.
chapters.title: Maxima Rodas shares nonbinary trans experience and supports Intro 134

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you, Chair Brooks Powers, the members of the Committee on Criminal Justice, and the New York City Council for holding this important hearing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: on interest 133 and 134, which will strengthen protection for transgenders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: Gender non-conforming, non-binary, and intersex people in the Department of Correction and Custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: My name is Maxima Rodas, and I'm a leader with the Trans Immigrant Project at Make the Road New York and several community organizations across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: I think everyone here will agree that the ideal scenario is to avoid incarceration altogether.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: But for many transgender, gender-expansive, and gender-diverse people like myself, our experiences with discrimination and policing can increase our vulnerability to the criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: For people like me who identify as non-binary and trans, being placed in a housing unit with people whose gender identity does not align with ours can be overwhelming and traumatic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: We should not have to give up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: Our dignity or sense of safety simply because we are in custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: That is why Introduction 134 is so important to me and why I'm here today to share my personal testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: The legislation will require the Department of Correction to consider a person's gender identity and personal sense of safety when making housing decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: It will also establish additional screening and a formal process to appeal housing decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: The mockery, abuse, and violence we face on the streets,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: in the shelter system, in public places, and even between our own families are already excessive and enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: It is unjust that on top of all of that,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: When we have the misfortune of being incarcerated, we suffer the same dehumanization and humiliation between the penal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: We urge the Council to pass Inches 133 and 134.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: And to ensure that transgender, gender nonconforming, nonbinary, and intersex people in custody are treated with dignity, respect, and humanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: Humanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maxima Rodas
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Danielle Regis of Brooklyn Defender Services says people often encounter police in crisis because appropriate care was inaccessible. She calls for individualized bail decisions and stronger access to low- and no-cost mental health and substance use treatment, saying jails are not therapeutic environments.
chapters.title: Danielle Regis urges bail reform and community mental health access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: My name is Danielle Regis, and I am a senior supervising attorney in the mental health representation team of the criminal defense practice at Brooklyn Defender Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Thank you to the Committee on Criminal Justice and Chair Brooks Powers for the opportunity to testify today about mental health care in the city jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: As a public defender, I have represented people in the Brooklyn Mental Health Court for nearly a decade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: The people I represent often encounter police when they are in crisis and seeking care, or when the absence of available care has led to the decompensation of their mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Too often, untreated mental illness becomes criminalized simply because the appropriate systems of care were not accessible when they were needed most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Jails are not therapeutic environments and are not appropriate settings for people to get meaningful mental health care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: In our written testimony, we highlight a number of concerns about mental health care provisions inside the city's jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: But in my limited time, I want to highlight some upstream solutions to prevent people with serious mental health needs from entering jails in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: First, bail amounts are regularly set without regard to what a person or their loved ones can afford.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Judges should make individualized decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: decisions when setting bail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Under state law, bail is a tool that should only be used to ensure people return to court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: In practice, judges routinely set money bail that functions as a detention order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Incarceration disconnects New Yorkers from their communities, resources, and support networks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: It means treatment, medication, and services are interrupted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Next, we urge this committee with the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use to address the gaps in access to low and no-cost mental health and substance use treatment in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Many of the people we represent have tried for years to access mental health and substance use treatment, but struggle to find providers who accept their insurance, speak their language, or have the skills needed to treat complex conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: They are often discharged from hospitals without proper follow-up care and lack appropriate resources in their communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: People seeking care remain on wait lists for months or years for assertive community treatment teams, supportive housing, psychiatric visits, or other care they require.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Individuals are routinely discharged from psychiatric hospitalization with nothing more than a referral.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The time has expired.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You could finish your sentence, though.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: I just want to say the city can no longer rely on a broken or dysfunctional jail system to serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: as the largest mental health treatment center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Danielle Regis
utterances.text: Thank you for your time, and I welcome any questions.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next, we will hear from Chris Payton.

chapters.summary: Chris Payton of Exodus Transitional Community says children of incarcerated parents experience grief, loss, confusion, shame, and trauma. He says referrals to community mental health should be available for children visiting incarcerated parents and cites CDC research on adverse childhood experiences.
chapters.title: Chris Payton supports Intro 453 referrals for children of incarcerated parents

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: My name is Chris Payton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: I'm the Associate Vice President of Behavioral Health at Exodus Transitional Community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: I'm a licensed clinical social worker and have been practicing for about 11 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: Along with this robust reentry trauma-focused programs, Exodus has the Genesis Clinic and Article 31 MOTAR's Mental Health Clinic in East Harlem, which I oversee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: I'm here today to speak about Bill Intro 453 to provide mental health services and referrals to children visiting incarcerated individuals in New York City jails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: Many of the patients we see at the Genesis Clinic are returning to society from incarceration, and many have children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: Anecdotally, our patients discuss the profound trauma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: Their children or those children they may have cared for prior to incarceration experienced because of their parents'caretakers'incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: A child is deeply affected by their parents'incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: As we know, when one person is incarcerated, it affects the entire family and community ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: When a parent is incarcerated, children can experience grief, loss, confusion, shame, financial hardship, family instability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: and the pain of having an important person in your life physically and emotionally absent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: For some children, visiting a loved one in jail may be the most difficult and traumatic experience in their life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: Trauma can show up as anxiety, depression, violence, anger, problems in school, distrusting others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: We know from the CDC's research of adverse childhood experiences that it can affect the developing child's brain immune system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Payton
utterances.text: So referrals to mental health in the community should be available for children incarcerated parents.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Sharon Content.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: If you are able to raise your hand to signal that you can hear us.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: All right, Sharon, try speaking one more time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We see your hand.

chapters.summary: Sharon Content, founder of Children of Promise NYC, says when a parent is incarcerated, the child serves a sentence too. She supports Intro 453 and urges that mental health support begin before a visit and continue after, addressing children's fear and confusion about correctional settings.
chapters.title: Sharon Content details trauma before and after visits for children

utterances.text: Okay, I was waiting for it to be unmuted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Good afternoon to Chair Brooks Powers, Council Member Stevens, and to the members of the Committee of Criminal Justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: My name is Sharon Content, and I'm the founder and president of Children of Promise NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: I seem to be a bit delayed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Are you guys, is everyone hearing me okay?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We can hear you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Okay, fabulous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: I am the founder and president of Children of Promise NYC, an organization that 17 years ago has worked specifically with children and families impacted by parental incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: I'm the founder of this organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: It is one that I have remained committed and passionate about from day one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: I want to thank you for the opportunity to speak today regarding Introduction 453-2026, which would establish a voluntary mental health services program for children under the age of 18

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: visiting individuals incarcerated in New York City jails, including referrals and whatever practical on-site mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: At Children of Promise NYC, we know firsthand when a parent is incarcerated, the child serves a sentence as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: The child may not be behind bars, but they experience the separation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: They experience unanswered questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: They exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: experience anxiety, fear, anger, shame, and sometimes the responsibility of trying to protect everyone around them while attempting to understand what is happening to their family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: When you ask that child to walk into a correctional facility to visit a parent they love,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Research shows that parental incarceration documents the emotional and behavioral challenges that can accompany parental incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: And it also shows the impact of visitation on children is complex.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: The quality of the visit, the environment surrounding it, and whenever appropriate, support is provided makes a significant difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: That is why the implementation of this legislation matters greatly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: From the experience of Children of Promise NYC, there are several elements that should be considered as this program is developed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: First, mental health support should begin before the visit, not after.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Not only after the child has visibly been distressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: A child may need to understand what they're about to see, what their facility will look like, why their parents are dressed differently, what security

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: procedures they may experience, and how they are feeling and seeing before leaving or while they're leaving their parent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Second, support you to continue after the visit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: For some children, the most difficult moment is walking away from the facility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Not only walking in, walking out is just as traumatic for our young person.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sharon, we're going to just ask you to wrap up.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You can submit the rest of the testimony in writing, though, but if you could close.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Children of Promise stands ready to share our experiences and work with the city to help develop a model that recognizes the child will simply, not as a visitor

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: to a correctional facility, but also as a young person trying to navigate one of the most complicated experiences a family can face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify this afternoon, most importantly, for centering the needs of children whose voices are too often absent from conversations around incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Content
utterances.text: Sharon Content, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Mar Henriquez of the Legal Aid Society LGBTQ Law and Policy Unit says DOC's testimony ignored the harms trans people face. Henriquez cites high rates of abuse, homelessness, and foster care among LGBTQ people and urges passage of Intros 133 and 134 to protect trans and gender nonconforming people in custody.
chapters.title: Mar Henriquez calls for Intros 133 and 134 and cites abuse statistics

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: Okay, we're ready.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: Hi, thank you so much for holding this hearing, and thank you so much, Council Member and Chair, for your support of Inter 133 and 134 and holding the space today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: I'd like to start by saying I'd like everyone here to imagine being locked and confined in a place where you're held against your will and your identity makes you a target.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: The people in charge are aware, and nothing is being done to stop it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: I sat here in dismay listening to DOC once again reiterate that they are doing everything as is required by law,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: and they're following PRIA guidelines, which is really disappointing to hear because, one, we know based on our clients, I work for the Legal Aid Society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: I've been with the Legal Aid Society for eight years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: In the LGBTQ law and policy unit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: And we see all too often how not only are humans completely disregarded for being incarcerated, but that is exacerbated by trans identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: And I'd like to run through some stats that highlight the precariousness of the situation that our clients and community members find themselves in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: So I'd like to iterate my support for 133, which would enable the task force to continue and encourage the amendments that will be introduced to be

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: enforced, but also highlighting 134, which was not added to the agenda, which is one of the top recommendations of the task force in actually addressing the harms that folks are experiencing on the inside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: We recognize, one, that 40% of New York City's runaway youth population are LGBTQ+.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: These numbers are only going to go up with the fact that on a federal level, people experiencing an inundated amount of attacks on their identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: The Lemkin Research Institute for Genocide has issued a third red flag because trans people are under attack in this country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: 31 to 46% of youth who exit foster care experience homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: We know that homelessness is criminalized in our communities, and that therefore leaves people susceptible and vulnerable to incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: The majority of our clients in the LGBTQ plus unit who are incarcerated made first contact with NYPD when they were minors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: These are people who are forgotten, who fell through the cracks because of lack of infrastructure, lack of familial support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: support and are then left to rot at Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: They, 90% of our clients report violent abuse in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: And this is just what's being reported.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: We should really assume it's 100% of folks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: So I'm really asking for folks to really advocate and continue to advocate for trans and gender nonconforming people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: There is a lack of understanding in our communities and that is state-sanctioned violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: From K through 12, we do not discuss trans and gender expansive identities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: People think that they're up for debate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: And then as a result, people are left to rot in prison and in jails and on the streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: And they deserve more and we deserve more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: And if we are to truly call ourselves a sanctuary city, we have to stand by our incarcerated population.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mar Henriquez
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

summary: The Committee on Criminal Justice held an oversight hearing on mental health care in New York City jails, also hearing Intros 133, 453, and 809.

Administration officials from Correctional Health Services and the Department of Correction testified on mental health screening, housing, treatment, reentry, lock-ins, and deadlocking; IBO presented analysis on mental illness and homelessness in custody.

Public defenders, advocates, directly impacted New Yorkers, and community providers testified, with many urging passage or amendment of Intros 133 and 453 and support for Intro 134; the committee also cast a roll-call vote on Intro 246A.
